portuguese-captives-1441.place: Rio do Ouro, West African coast, and Portugal
portuguese-captives-1441.summary: In 1441 Prince Henry sent the young captain Antão Gonçalves to the West African coast for seal skins and oil; Gonçalves resolved to take captives as well and, with Nuno Tristão, carried the first captives from the Rio do Ouro region back to Portugal.

Having taken that cargo, Gonçalves called together the one and twenty men of his ship and said, in Zurara's account: “O How fair a thing it would be if we, who have come to this land for a cargo of such petty merchandise, were to meet with the good luck to bring the first captives before the face of our Prince.” He then went inland by night with nine men to find inhabitants to seize.

Wikipedia's summary of Zurara's chronicle says Gonçalves captured a man and a woman; joining with Nuno Tristão's crew, they captured ten more, among them a nobleman named Adahu. Gonçalves returned to Portugal and in 1442 sailed again with the nobleman, whom he exchanged for ten slaves, some gold dust and ostrich eggs.

Almost three hundred years later the authorisation to take non-Christian lands was cited by U.S. Chief Justice John Marshall in shaping the discovery doctrine; in 2023 the Vatican named Inter Caetera among the bulls behind the 'doctrine of discovery' and repudiated the doctrine.

taino-population-collapse.summary: Under war, enslavement, famine, the mines and epidemic disease, the Taíno of Hispaniola fell from a pre-contact population variously estimated up to the millions to about 60,000 by 1507–1508, some 26,000–32,000 in 1514, and 200 by 1565.
account: Estimates of the Taíno population of Hispaniola before 1492 vary widely, from 10,000 to 1,000,000 in one source read; Las Casas wrote that from 1494 to 1508 'over three million people had perished from war, slavery and the mines'. Researchers today doubt his figures.

When some Taíno refused to plant, food became so scarce in 1495 and 1496 that some 50,000 died of famine. Forced into the mines through the encomienda, the population of about 400,000 was reduced to 60,000 by 1508 (60,000 by 1507 in another account); by 1514 only 26,334 remained, or about 32,000 by another report. By 1565 there were 200. Scholars hold epidemic disease (smallpox, influenza, measles, typhus) to have been an overwhelming cause alongside forced labour.

Spanish documents declared the Taíno extinct as early as 1550, and in 1802 the colonial authorities officially declared them extinct; mixed-race and other Taíno descendants continue to live. Census records from 1514 show that 40 percent of Spanish men on Hispaniola had Taíno wives.

Las Casas, who had come with Ponce de León to Puerto Rico, protested the Spanish treatment of the Taíno at court in 1512. When colonists complained that they needed labour for the mines, forts and sugar, Las Casas suggested African slaves instead, and in 1517 the Crown permitted its subjects to import twelve slaves each. In early writings Las Casas advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour; later in life he repented, judging 'black slavery … as unjust as Indian slavery'.

The first asiento was drawn up in August 1518, giving Charles I's Flemish favourite Laurent de Gouvenot a monopoly on importing enslaved Africans for eight years, to a maximum of 4,000; he sold it to Genoese merchants for 25,000 ducats. From 1525 slaves were carried directly from São Tomé across the Atlantic to Hispaniola.

encomienda-new-laws-1503-1545.summary: From 1503 the Spanish Crown granted conquistadors encomiendas, the labour of whole Indigenous communities; the New Laws of 20 November 1542 limited them, but the restriction was repealed in 1545 after the encomenderos resisted.
account: Governor Nicolás de Ovando set up the formal encomienda on Hispaniola. Although Isabella I had declared the natives free vassals of the Crown in 1501, in 1503 the Crown began formally granting encomiendas to conquistadors and officials as rewards: a monopoly on the labour of particular Indigenous groups, which devolved into a form of communal slavery. Natives were forced into hard labour and punished, even killed, if they resisted.

Following the protests of Bartolomé de las Casas and others, Charles V issued the New Laws on 20 November 1542 to limit the encomenderos' power; encomiendas were to end on the holder's death. The encomenderos resisted: in Peru Gonzalo Pizarro led a revolt, and the first viceroy, Blasco Núñez Vela, was killed in 1546. The laws, passed in 1542, were repealed in 1545. The encomienda was legally ended only in 1720.

Isabella and Ferdinand authorised it in 1503 to reward the conquistadors and force conversion to Catholicism; Columbus had already begun the forced labour in 1492–93. ponce-de-leon-conquers-borinquen-1508.summary: In 1508 Juan Ponce de León led the first official Spanish expedition to Puerto Rico, founded Caparra, became governor in 1509 and parcelled out the Taíno among the settlers in encomienda to mine gold and grow food.
account: Ponce de León had first seen the island on Columbus's second voyage in 1493 and had helped crush a Taíno rebellion on Hispaniola. In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to the island the Spanish called San Juan Bautista; about 50 men in one ship left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 and anchored in San Juan Bay, and placer gold was found in the west of the island. Archival documents suggest an earlier, quieter expedition as early as 1506.

He built a storehouse and fortified house about two miles from the bay, the first settlement, Caparra, in late 1508; it is a U.S. National Historic Landmark, the oldest known European settlement in the United States. Ovando appointed him governor, confirmed by Ferdinand II on 14 August 1509, with instructions to extend the settlement and continue mining for gold.

Ponce de León parcelled out the native Taínos among himself and other settlers under the forced-labour system of encomienda, putting them to work growing food and mining gold; his own encomienda searched for gold in the Toa Valley. Many Spaniards treated the Taínos very harshly and death rates were very high, and the demand for slaves kidnapped from other islands grew. By June 1511 the Taínos began a rebellion, put down by Ponce de León with crossbows and arquebuses. A 1530 story from Caparra tells of two Spaniards each with 40 Taíno slaves searching the rivers for gold.

account: Hatuey, a Taíno cacique from Hispaniola, crossed to Cuba with a party of four hundred in canoes ahead of Diego Velázquez's 1511 expedition to warn the people of eastern Cuba what to expect from the Spaniards. He fought by guerrilla tactics and killed at least eight Spanish soldiers; using mastiffs and torturing the Indigenous for information, the Spaniards captured him.

On 2 February 1512 he was tied to a stake and burned alive at Yara, near present-day Bayamo. Las Casas records that when a priest asked if he would accept Jesus and go to heaven, Hatuey asked whether Spaniards went to heaven and, told yes, said he did not want to go there but to hell, so as not to see such cruel people. He is remembered as Cuba's first national hero.

velazquez-conquest-of-cuba-and-caonao-15.place: Baracoa, Bayamo, Caonao (Camagüey) and Havana, Cuba
velazquez-conquest-of-cuba-and-caonao-15.summary: Diego Velázquez sailed from Hispaniola in January 1511 with about 300 men, defeated the Taíno resistance, founded Baracoa and six more towns by 1515, and apportioned the Native people in encomienda; Las Casas witnessed the massacre of the people of Caonao.
account: Las Casas estimated the Taíno population of Cuba at 350,000 by the end of the 15th century. Velázquez sailed for Cuba in January 1511 with four ships and 300 men, among them Hernán Cortés and Pedro de Alvarado, and landed in the province of Mayci. The Taínos, organized by the cacique Hatuey, were outmatched by Spanish weapons and defeated after two months of intermittent fighting. Baracoa was founded by August 1511, and Pánfilo de Narváez brought thirty Spanish archers and Native auxiliaries from Jamaica; within three years the Spanish controlled the island.

Las Casas observed a number of massacres, notably near Camagüey of the inhabitants of Caonao: by his account some three thousand villagers who had come to greet the Spanish with food were "without provocation, butchered". Survivors fled to the mountains or small islands before being captured and forced into reservations such as Guanabacoa.

In 1513 Ferdinand II decreed the encomienda system, and Velázquez apportioned the land and the Indigenous peoples among the colonists. Bayamo was founded in 1513 and Trinidad, Sancti Spíritus and Havana in 1514; gold deposits set off a gold rush until about 1520. The native population was largely destroyed as a culture after 1550; under the New Laws of 1552 Indigenous Cubans were freed from encomienda.

Ponce de León led a series of offensives that culminated in the Battle of Yagüecas, where some 11,000 to 15,000 Taíno faced some 80 to 100 Spaniards; a Spanish arquebusier shot a native wearing a cacique's golden necklace, presumed to be Agüeybaná II. spanish-conquest-of-guatemala-1524.place: Guatemalan Highlands and western El Salvador
spanish-conquest-of-guatemala-1524.summary: Sent by Hernán Cortés, Pedro de Alvarado invaded the Maya kingdoms of Guatemala in 1524, burned the Kʼicheʼ kings alive and their capital Qʼumarkaj, and campaigned against the Pipil of Cuzcatlán in present-day El Salvador until 1528.
account: Cortés despatched Pedro de Alvarado with 180 cavalry, 300 infantry, crossbows, muskets, 4 cannons and thousands of allied warriors from Tlaxcala, Cholula and other cities of central Mexico; they arrived in Soconusco in 1523. A Kʼicheʼ army was defeated in the Quetzaltenango valley in February 1524 and many Kʼicheʼ nobles were among the dead; local tradition places the death of the prince Tecun Uman in these battles.

In March 1524 Alvarado entered Qʼumarkaj, the Kʼicheʼ capital, at the invitation of its remaining lords. He seized the king Oxib-Keh and the king-elect Beleheb-Tzy in his camp, had the captured lords burnt to death, and then burned the entire city. He then demanded gold in tribute from the Kaqchikel, and by 1526 rebellions had engulfed the highlands. Bartolomé de las Casas charged him with further atrocities in the conquest of the Maya kingdoms.

The same year Alvarado led an expedition against the Pipil province of Cuzcatlán but retreated to Guatemala by July 1524. San Salvador, founded in 1525, was destroyed in a native rising in 1526; Alvarado campaigned again in 1526 and 1528, and the uprising ended in 1528 when the Spanish stormed the native stronghold at the Peñol de Cinacantan. The conquest of Guatemala's other peoples went on until the Petén fell in 1697. Disease, chiefly smallpox and measles, is counted at 1,600,000 dead between 1525 and 1550, and an estimated 33–50% of the highland population perished.

It was Pedro the conquistador; Cortés, Pizarro and Pedro, all the conquistadors who came from 1492, are the wicked of that verse, and it was the Spaniard, not the Chinese or the Arab, who covered the faces of the judges and changed the face of Christ, and who put the churches all over this country.

account: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba set out from Panama for Nicaragua in mid-October 1523 under orders of Pedrarias Dávila, the governor of Castilla del Oro, with over 200 men, including Hernando de Soto, and approximately 16 African slaves. In 1524 he founded León and Granada. Spanish records show that as early as 1524 prisoners of war were being shipped to Panama as slaves. Pedrarias himself governed Nicaragua from 1528 until his death at León Viejo in 1531.

The population of Nicaragua at the time of contact is estimated at 825,000. The first century after Spanish contact saw the demographic collapse of the native populations, resulting principally from Old World diseases and their exportation as slaves, and also from war and mistreatment; within a century of the conquest the native inhabitants of the Pacific region had been nearly exterminated.

afonso-kongo-letter-1526.summary: In 1526 Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, wrote to the king of Portugal that traders were kidnapping his people, even nobles and his own family, and branding them, and that his land was being depopulated.
account: Mvemba a Nzinga, Afonso I, ruled Kongo from 1509 to 1542 or 1543 and made Christianity the royal faith. To pay for Portuguese imports some Kongolese nobles illegally exported slaves, some kidnapping and enslaving freeborn Kongolese, and in 1526 Afonso issued a letter protesting the circumvention of Kongolese law.

He wrote to the king of Portugal: “Each day the traders are kidnapping our people – children of this country, sons of our nobles and vassals, even people of our own family. This corruption and depravity are so widespread that our land is entirely depopulated. … It is our wish that this Kingdom not be a place for the trade or transport of slaves.” He added that as soon as the captives were in the hands of white men they were branded with a red-hot iron.

Afonso threatened to end the trade if Portugal did not regulate its merchants, and set up a committee of Kongolese and Portuguese merchants to judge whether each person sold had been lawfully enslaved.

estevanico-1528-1539.summary: Esteban, an enslaved 'Arabic-speaking black man' from Azemmour, Morocco, survived the 1528 Narváez expedition, crossed some 2,000 miles of North America with three companions by 1536, and in 1539 guided the expedition to Cíbola, where he was killed.
account: Esteban de Dorantes, called Estevanico the Moor, was described as a 'negro alárabe', an Arabic-speaking black man, from Azemmour in Morocco; in 1522 he was sold as a slave to the Spanish nobleman Andrés Dorantes de Carranza. From 1528 he took part in the Narváez expedition to Florida, which ended in shipwreck and captivity.

With three other survivors he escaped in 1534 and became a medicine man; together they travelled nearly 2,000 miles through the American interior, the first non-Natives to enter the American West and Pueblo lands, reaching a Spanish settlement in Sinaloa in July 1536. In 1539 he guided Fray Marcos de Niza's expedition in search of the Seven Cities of Cíbola, went ahead of the main party and was killed at Cíbola (Hawikuh). He is believed to be the first person of African and Arab descent to explore what is now the United States, after Juan Garrido.

The best known of the early black explorers was Estevanico, who opened up New Mexico and Arizona for the Spaniards; another, with De Soto, stayed among the Indians in Alabama and became the first settler from the Old World.

inquisition-new-spain-1528-1596.summary: In 1528 the conquistador Hernando Alonso, a converso who had built the brigantines for the siege of Tenochtitlan, was burned at the stake in Mexico on charges of Judaizing; the Holy Office was established in New Spain on 4 November 1571, and on 8 December 1596 nine members of the Carvajal circle were burned.
account: Hernando Alonso, one of the shipbuilders who built the brigs for the siege of Tenochtitlan, was arrested in 1528 on charges of Judaizing, tortured until he confessed, and burned at the stake; he was the first person burned at the stake in the New World, and his brother Gonzalo de Morales was burned the same day. A historian judged the charges likely based on partly fabricated evidence.

In the 1530s Bishop Juan de Zumárraga exercised inquisitorial powers, prosecuting Nahua lords such as Don Carlos Ometochtzin, who was burned at the stake. The Tribunal of the Holy Office in New Spain was established on 4 November 1571 and lasted until 1820; about 50 people are estimated to have been executed, 29 of them as 'Judaizers' between 1571 and 1700 out of 324 prosecuted.

On 8 December 1596 most of the extended family of Luis de Carvajal y de la Cueva, including his sister Francisca and her children, nine people in all, were tortured and burned. A plaque at the convent of San Diego marks the quemadero, the burning place, used from 1596 to 1771.

brazil-sugar-african-slavery.summary: From the 1530s the Portuguese built a sugar economy in Brazil; after trying Indigenous labour, from the 1570s they made enslaved Africans, many shipped from Luanda, the labour force of the sugar plantations.
account: In 1530 Martim Afonso de Sousa's expedition founded the first colonial villages such as São Vicente. Pernambuco, Duarte Coelho's captaincy (Olinda founded 1536), prospered with sugar mills (engenhos) installed after 1542, and sugar became Brazil's main colonial product for the next 150 years; the first sugarcane farms were established in the mid-sixteenth century.

The Portuguese first used Indigenous slaves for sugar, then shifted to enslaved Africans: starting in the 1570s, African slaves became the labour force of choice on the sugar plantations, though Indigenous enslavement continued, as many as 40,000 natives having perhaps been taken from the interior by 1580. Sugar was the colony's primary export from 1600 to 1650, and many of the enslaved were embarked at West Central African ports, especially Luanda.

That labour fuelled the economy of Brazil and the old American South.

portuguese-inquisition-1536.summary: After years of pressure from John III, Pope Paul III established the Portuguese Inquisition on 23 May 1536; its main target was the New Christians suspected of secretly practising Judaism, and its first auto de fe was held in 1540.
account: In December 1531 Pope Clement VII granted permission for an inquisition in Portugal on conditions the king would not accept, and in 1535 suspended it. After long negotiations, Paul III's bull Cum ad nihil magis established the Portuguese Inquisition on 23 May 1536, at the request of King John III.

Its major target was the New Christians, many of them Spanish Jews who had fled to Portugal, suspected of secretly practising Judaism. It held its first auto de fe in 1540 and spread its operations to Brazil, Cape Verde and India. Between 1540 and 1794 its tribunals in Lisbon, Porto, Coimbra and Évora burned 1,175 people, burned 633 in effigy and penanced 29,590; another estimate puts its victims between 1540 and 1765 at around 40,000.

siege-of-cusco-1536.summary: Manco Inca, the Sapa Inca the Spaniards had crowned and then imprisoned and humiliated, escaped in April 1536 and laid a ten-month siege to Cusco, which the Spaniards held; when it failed he withdrew to Vilcabamba.
account: After Pizarro's men captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca and killed him in July 1533, taking a ransom of over 39,000 lb (18 t) of gold and silver, they captured Cusco on November 15, 1533 and had Manco Inca crowned. Real power rested with the Spaniards, who frequently humiliated him; Juan Pizarro imprisoned him after an attempted escape in November 1535.

Released in January 1536, Manco left Cusco on April 18, 1536, met his military chiefs at Lares, and gathered an army estimated at 100,000 to 200,000 men (some sources say as few as 40,000) around the city, held by 190 Spaniards and several thousand Indian auxiliaries. The Incas seized the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above the city on May 5, 1536; the siege began on 6 May and lasted until March 1537.

Manco coordinated it with a siege of Lima under his captain Quiso Yupanqui; the Incas defeated four relief expeditions sent by Francisco Pizarro, killing nearly 500 Spanish soldiers. When the siege failed, Manco withdrew to Ollantaytambo and then to the remote jungles of Vilcabamba, where he founded the Neo-Inca State in 1537.

lempira-and-the-lenca-rising-1537.summary: In 1537 the Lenca war captain Lempira united Lenca towns against Francisco de Montejo's conquest of Honduras and held the Peñol de Cerquín for months before the Spaniards killed him; he is regarded by the people as a warrior hero whom the conquistadors feared.
account: Based at the hill of Cerquín, Lempira organized resistance against the Spanish in 1537, gathering an army of almost 30,000 soldiers from 200 villages; other groups in the valleys of Comayagua and Olancho also took up arms. Spanish attempts to stop him, led by Francisco de Montejo and Alonso de Cáceres, were unsuccessful until later in 1537.

Accounts of his death differ. Antonio de Herrera's history (1626) says the Spaniards lured him out to talk and a concealed soldier shot him with an arquebus, after which the Lenca surrendered; this is the version taught in Honduran schools. In April 1537 they beat the psihipqua Tisquesusa at Funza; in the Iraka Valley the iraca Sugamuxi fell, and the Sun Temple was burned by two of Quesada's soldiers in early September. On August 6, 1538 Quesada founded Bogotá as the capital of the New Kingdom of Granada; Tisquesusa's successor Sagipa allied with the Spanish that month. The conquest lasted until 1540.

Over six years he killed, tortured and enslaved thousands of natives; his policy was to "terrorize the natives with often unprovoked killing, torture, and enslavement", and the Spanish tried to force the natives into servitude through the encomienda.

In spring 1540 the Caxcanes struck back. The spark was apparently the arrest of eighteen native leaders and the hanging of nine of them; many fled the encomiendas to the hill fortress of Mixtón in Zacatecas. Led by Francisco Tenamaztle, the rising was put down by Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza with Tlaxcalan and Mexica allies by 1542; Pedro de Alvarado was killed in the campaign.

Michimalonco's brother Trangolonco revolted and destroyed the Spanish settlement at Marga Marga, and the chiefs of the Cachapoal, Maipo and Mapocho valleys gathered around 16,000 warriors. On September 11, 1541 Michimalonco carried out the Destruction of Santiago, with only a handful of Spaniards barely surviving, and then waged an 'empty war' of starving the Spaniards of food. The Spanish finished controlling the valleys of Cachapoal, Maipo and Aconcagua at the end of 1543; in 1544 Michimalonco, with Diaguita allies, tried to cut the land route to Peru and was defeated at Limarí. The same year the Arauco War with the Mapuche began at the Bío-Bío River.

cocoliztli-epidemics-1545-1576.summary: Waves of a hemorrhagic fever the Aztecs called cocoliztli, 'pestilence', killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people in sixteenth-century New Spain; it fell most heavily on the Indigenous people.
account: The cocoliztli epidemic, an illness of high fevers and bleeding, caused 5–15 million deaths in New Spain during the 16th century and is often called the worst epidemic in Mexico's history. Its largest outbreaks were in 1545 and 1576; a second large outbreak in 1576 lasted until about 1580 and caused approximately two million deaths. Spanish accounts cite 13 cocoliztli epidemics between 1545 and 1642.

Researchers disagree on the cause: genomic studies point to Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, while others propose an Indigenous viral hemorrhagic fever worsened by drought and by the poor living conditions of the Indigenous peoples after the conquest. The encomendero Gonzalo de Ortiz wrote that God sent such sickness on the Indians that three out of every four perished; the modern consensus is that Indigenous people were the most affected.

potosi-and-the-mita.summary: Silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí in 1545; from 1573 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo drafted one in seven adult native men into the mines through the mita, a forced-labour system under which many died and whole communities fled.
account: Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, is credited with discovering the Cerro Rico in 1545. Potosí grew to more than 200,000 people, and the mountain produced an estimated 60% of all the silver mined in the world in the second half of the 16th century; the Spanish still say valer un Potosí, 'to be worth a Potosí'. From 1554 the patio process used mercury to extract the silver, and mercury poisoning took the lives of many in the refining.

The Spanish Crown repurposed the Andean mit'a in 1573. Under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, sent to Peru in 1569, communities had to provide one seventh of their male labour force; the first mit'a recruits reached Potosí in 1573, and recruitment came to cover nearly 200,000 square miles of southern Peru and present-day Bolivia. Thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year. Mitayos carried loads of 100 to 300 lbs up ladders in narrow shafts; many died or were seriously injured, and assignment to the mines was considered worse than a death sentence.

Thousands fled their villages and forfeited their land to escape the draft; by the late 17th century Upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its indigenous population compared with a little over a century earlier. A 1603 report counted 58,800 Indians working at Potosí, 5,100 of them mitayos. Potosí was a multiracial society of native Andeans, Spanish settlers and black slaves.

A typhus plague, drought and famine kept the Mapuche from driving the Spaniards out in 1554 and 1555; in 1556–1557 Lautaro tried to reach Santiago to free central Chile and was killed in an ambush in 1557. He is revered among Mapuche and non-Mapuche Chileans and Argentinians.

friars-israelite-origin-1581-1607.summary: Spanish writers of the sixteenth century, among them the Dominican Diego Durán in his History of the Indies of New Spain (c.1581), discussed the theory that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were of Israelite descent; in 1607 the Dominican Gregorio García published the first systematic treatment of it.
account: Diego Durán (c.1537–1588), a Dominican born in Seville and raised in Texcoco, was fluent in Nahuatl and consulted natives and Aztec codices; his History of the Indies of New Spain was completed in about 1581. The theory that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were of Israelite descent was discussed by Spanish writers in the sixteenth century, including Diego de Landa (around 1566) and Durán's History (1581).

The first systematic treatment came in 1607 with The Origin of the Indians of the New World by the Dominican Gregorio García, who argued that the lost tribes of Israel travelled to the Americas alongside other migrations (Carthaginians, Phoenicians, people from China, Tartary and Atlantis), that 'Mex-' in Mexico came from the Hebrew word for Messiah, and that circumcision was common among the natives, particularly in Yucatán.

fall-of-vilcabamba-and-tupac-amaru-1572.summary: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo declared war on the last Inca state at Vilcabamba in April 1572; its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, was hunted down, tried and beheaded in the main square of Cusco on September 24, 1572, ending the Inca state.
account: The Neo-Inca State founded by Manco Inca at Vilcabamba in 1537 lasted until 1572. When two Spanish ambassadors were killed on its border, Toledo declared war on 14 April 1572; the Spanish entered the deserted city on 24 June. Túpac Amaru fled into the lowland forests with about 100 people, and a group of forty soldiers under Martín García Óñez de Loyola pursued and arrested him with his wife.

The captives were marched into Cuzco on 21 September with the mummified remains of Manco Cápac and Titu Cusi. Five Inca generals were sentenced to hanging; Túpac Amaru was convicted of the murder of priests and sentenced to be beheaded. Clerics pleaded on their knees that he be sent to Spain instead, and Philip II disapproved of the execution. Before 10,000 to 15,000 witnesses in the main square of Cuzco, his reported last words were: 'Pacha Kamaq, witness how my enemies shed my blood.'

account: The Pequot War was fought from 1636 to 1638 between the Pequot nation and the Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Saybrook colonists with their Narragansett and Mohegan allies. On the night of May 26, 1637 a Connecticut force under Captain John Mason, joined by Captain John Underhill and allied Natives, surrounded the fortified Pequot village near the Mystic River; Mason ordered it set ablaze and its two exits blocked, and those who tried to escape over the palisade were shot or killed outside. barbados-sugar-slave-code-1661.summary: Barbados's planters switched from tobacco and indentured European labour to sugar in the 1640s, and the enslaved African population tripled; in 1661 the island's parliament passed "An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes," the first comprehensive slave code in English America, which classed enslaved people as chattel property and became the model for later codes elsewhere.
account: Barbadian planters took up sugar cultivation in the 1640s, replacing tobacco and indentured European workers with enslaved Africans; the enslaved population on the island tripled over the decade as the sugar plantations grew.

In 1661 the Parliament of Barbados passed "An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes," the first comprehensive slave code in English America. Its preamble classed enslaved people as "chattel property," required masters to provide only one set of clothing a year with no standard for diet or housing, and let an owner mutilate or burn a slave alive without legal consequence; an enslaved person who struck a white person could be whipped, have the nose slit and the face branded, and be put to death for a second offence.

Historian Russell Menard writes that because Barbados was the first English colony to write a comprehensive slave code, its code was especially influential: Jamaica, South Carolina (1696), Antigua and other colonies adopted or modelled their own slave codes on it, and its influence is traceable even where Virginia's and Maryland's codes were not exact copies.

code-noir-1685.summary: In March 1685 King Louis XIV of France issued the Code Noir, a 60-article royal decree that legalized and regulated slavery across the French Caribbean colonies, including Saint-Domingue, where it took effect May 6, 1687.
account: The Code Noir was promulgated by Louis XIV in March 1685 to govern slavery in France's Caribbean colonies. It was implemented in Martinique on August 6, 1685, Guadeloupe on December 10, 1685, and Saint-Domingue on May 6, 1687; it was later extended to Louisiana (1724) and the Mascarene Islands (1723). Its first article ordered all Jews expelled from the colonies within three months.

The code required enslaved people to be baptized and instructed in the Catholic faith, gave them Sundays and Catholic holy days as rest days, and specified minimum food and clothing. It forbade them to carry weapons, assemble in groups, work on Sundays, or practice any religion but Catholicism, and barred their testimony as legal proof, though they could lodge complaints of mistreatment. Punishments were severe: ear-cropping for a first escape attempt, hamstringing for a second, and death for a third; masters could beat enslaved people but not torture or mutilate them outside the code's own penalties, and killing an enslaved person was technically prosecutable.

account: In 1736 Antigua's authorities said they had discovered a conspiracy led by an enslaved man called Prince Klaas (recorded as "Court" and also called Tackey), said to have been born around 1690 in what is now Ghana and brought to Antigua around 1701. The plan, as the governor described it, was to smuggle a ten-gallon barrel of gunpowder into a building and detonate it during a ball honouring King George II in late October 1736, killing the Europeans gathered there and signalling enslaved people on the surrounding plantations to rise and kill the white population, with the aim of establishing an African-governed state.

On the report of an enslaved informer, Klaas and 132 others were tried. Eighty-eight were executed: 77, including Klaas, were broken on the wheel or burned at the stake, and 6 were gibbeted (left to die in a metal cage); other accounts give 6 hanged and starved and 58 burned at the stake. Klaas was about 45 when he was executed in early November 1736. Some historians have questioned whether the colony's magistrates, in a state of panic, exaggerated or invented the scale of the plot.

stono-rebellion-1739.summary: On 9 September 1739 enslaved Africans led by a literate man named Jemmy rose near the Stono River in South Carolina and marched south toward Spanish Florida; it was the largest slave rebellion of the Southern colonial era.

They recruited nearly 60 others and killed more than 20 whites before the South Carolina militia intercepted them near the Edisto River. In all 25 colonists and 35 to 50 Africans were killed. Most of the captured were executed and the few survivors sold to the West Indies. The General Assembly answered with the Negro Act of 1740.

guarani-war-1754-1756.place: Misiones Orientales, east of the Uruguay River
guarani-war-1754-1756.summary: When the 1750 Treaty of Madrid gave the seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River to Portugal, their Guaraní refused to leave; a joint Spanish–Portuguese army defeated them at Caiboaté on February 10, 1756, killing 1,511 Guaraní for four European dead.
account: The Treaty of Madrid set the Uruguay River as the border between Spanish and Portuguese territory, and the seven missions east of it, with 26,362 inhabitants by a Jesuit census, were to be dismantled and moved west. For most of the missions' history the Guaraní had fought Luso-Brazilian slavers, the bandeirantes, who sought to capture them to sell in Brazil.

In 1754 the Jesuits surrendered the missions, but the Guaraní, led by Sepé Tiaraju, refused to relocate; Spanish and Portuguese forces sent in July 1754 failed to remove them. On 10 February 1756, 3,000 Spanish and Portuguese soldiers fought the Guaraní at Caiboaté: 1,511 Guaraní were killed and four Europeans. The army occupied the seven missions; Spain and Portugal annulled the treaty in 1761.

tackys-revolt-jamaica-1760.place: St. Mary and Westmoreland parishes, Jamaica
tackys-revolt-jamaica-1760.summary: On Easter Monday, 7 April 1760, an enslaved Fante leader named Tacky led an uprising in Jamaica that seized plantations and a fort before being put down over many months; a second rising broke out in the west under Apongo in May, and scattered guerrilla resistance continued into 1761.
account: On 7 April 1760, Tacky, a Fante royal from present-day Ghana enslaved on a Jamaican plantation, led an uprising that captured the Frontier and Trinity plantations and took nearly four barrels of gunpowder and 40 firearms from Fort Haldane. In May a second rising broke out in Westmoreland led by Apongo. British forces, helped by Jamaican Maroons bound by treaty to suppress revolts, hunted down the rebels; a Maroon marksman named Davy shot Tacky dead, and his head was displayed on a pole in Spanish Town.

About 60 white colonists and 60 free Black people were killed in the uprising; more than 1,100 rebels were killed and over 500 were captured and resold into slavery elsewhere. The revolt fragmented into guerrilla raids from the Cockpit Country that continued through 1761. The colonial assembly passed harsher slave laws afterward and banned the practice of Obeah.

cuba-sugar-boom-and-slave-trade-1762-186.place: Havana, Santiago de Cuba and the sugar districts of western Cuba
cuba-sugar-boom-and-slave-trade-1762-186.summary: After the British occupation of Havana in 1762 and the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became one of the world's largest sugar producers on enslaved African labour; more than a million Africans were brought to the island, and the trade went on until 1867, decades after Spain agreed to end it.
account: Since the 1550s the Spaniards had relied on the Taíno for enslaved labour; as the Indigenous population declined from disease and warfare they introduced the chattel slavery of West Africans. Just over 40,000 enslaved people had been imported to the island in the 250 years before 1762.

In 1762 British forces under the Earl of Albemarle captured Havana and, during a year-long occupation, expanded the plantation system and imported 4,000 enslaved people from the British West Indies. Santiago de Cuba was authorized from 1789 as a port of arrival for the transatlantic trade. After the Haitian Revolution, Cuba's planters took much of the sugar market formerly held by Saint-Domingue and greatly expanded their imports from Africa: between 1791 and 1805, 91,211 enslaved people entered through Havana.

An Anglo-Spanish treaty of 1817 gained Spain's agreement to end the trade north of the Equator, but 372,449 enslaved people were imported before the trade legally ended and at least 123,775 between 1821 and 1853; lax enforcement brought an estimated 90,000 from 1856 to 1860. The Cuban trade continued until 1867. In all, more than a million enslaved Africans were brought to Cuba, from over 20 African peoples, chief among them Lucumí (Yoruba), Mandingo, Ganga, Arará, Carabalí and Congo.

On the sugar plantations, work days lasted close to 20 hours at harvest; the enslaved were locked at night in barracoons, put in stocks for days or months, and whipped, pregnant women included. The Spanish Black Code of 1789 limited lashings to 25, but planters flouted it.

fort-pitt-smallpox-blankets-1763.summary: During Pontiac’s War, the officers at besieged Fort Pitt gave Native emissaries two blankets and a handkerchief from the fort’s smallpox hospital on June 24, 1763, while the commander-in-chief Jeffery Amherst proposed sending smallpox among the tribes.

On June 24 Turtleheart told the garrison that the other forts had fallen and warned it to leave; William Trent and Alexander McKee thanked him and presented the delegates with two small blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital.

Writing to Colonel Henry Bouquet on about June 29, 1763, Jeffery Amherst asked: “Could it not be contrived to send the smallpox among the disaffected tribes of Indians?” In a postscript of July 13 Bouquet wrote that he would try to inoculate the Indians by means of blankets. adair-history-of-the-american-indians-17.summary: In 1775 James Adair, a trader who lived among the Southeastern nations for decades, published The History of the American Indians, half of which argues that the American Indians are descended from the Israelites.
account: Adair, born in Ireland about 1709, came to South Carolina in 1735, traded with the Catawba and Cherokee and from 1744 lived chiefly among the Chickasaw. He compiled his notes into a book published in London in 1775 by Edward and Charles Dilly.

The first part of the book is “Observations, and arguments in proof of the American Indians being descended from the Jews”, a series of numbered arguments beginning with the division into tribes. Among the likenesses Adair pressed were tribes, worship of Jehovah, theocracy, laws of uncleanness, cities of refuge, divorce and raising seed to a deceased brother.

The second part is an account of the Katahba, Cheerake, Muskohge, Choktah and Chikkasah nations. Later writers both championed and condemned the Israelite theory; a German translation appeared in 1782.

That is what happened to the tribe of Gad that is called the American Indians.

great-hurricane-of-1780.summary: The Great Hurricane of 9–18 October 1780 tore through the Lesser Antilles with winds estimated near 200 mph, killing about 22,000 people across Barbados, St. Lucia, Martinique and other islands, making it the deadliest hurricane recorded in the Atlantic; enslaved plantation labourers, housed in the flimsiest buildings and given no warning, made up the great majority of the dead.
account: The Great Hurricane struck the Lesser Antilles from 9 to 18 October 1780, reaching Barbados on 10 October with gusts estimated at 200 mph, then moving through St. Vincent, St. Lucia, Martinique, St. Eustatius, Dominica and on to Puerto Rico and Bermuda.

The storm killed roughly 22,000 people in total, the highest death toll of any Atlantic hurricane on record: about 4,300 in Barbados, 6,000 in St. Lucia, 9,000 in Martinique and 4,000–5,000 on St. Eustatius. Martinique's capital, St. Pierre, was almost completely demolished, and a 20-foot storm surge struck St. Vincent. Warring British and French fleets in the region at the time added to the toll.

rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii-1780.place: Cusco, Tinta and the southern Andes, Peru
rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii-1780.summary: In November 1780 the kuraka José Gabriel Condorcanqui, taking the name Túpac Amaru II, led Quechua, Aymara and mestizo rebels against Spanish rule and the forced labour of the mita; he was captured and torn apart in Cusco on May 18, 1781, and the rising went on to 1783 at a cost estimated at 100,000 indigenous dead.
account: The rebellion arose against the Bourbon Reforms, which among other things forced the indigenous population to mine under the mita, largely at the Cerro Rico of Potosí; among Túpac Amaru II's proclamations were the freedom of the indigenous people and the abolition of slavery. It began on 4 November 1780 with the seizure of the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, hanged on 10 November before thousands.

Betrayed after defeats at Combapata and Checacupe in April 1781, Túpac Amaru II was sentenced on 15 May and on 18 May forced to watch the execution of his wife, Micaela Bastidas, and one of his children; four horses failed to tear his limbs apart, and he was beheaded in the Plaza de Armas of Cusco. His relatives and Túpac Katari carried on until 1783. The death toll is estimated at 100,000 indigenous people and 10,000–40,000 non-natives. It was the largest revolt in the Americas before the Spanish American wars of independence and the Haitian Revolution.

tupac-katari-and-the-siege-of-la-paz-178.place: La Paz and El Alto, Upper Peru (Bolivia)
tupac-katari-and-the-siege-of-la-paz-178.summary: The Aymara leader Túpac Katari raised some 40,000 men and besieged La Paz from March 1781; the siege was broken in October, and he was captured and executed by quartering in November 1781, with his wife Bartolina Sisa and his sister Gregoria Apaza later executed too.
account: Julián Apasa took the name Túpac Katari to honour the rebels Tomás Katari and Túpac Amaru. In 1781 he raised an army of some 40,000 and laid siege to La Paz on 13 March, holding court with his wife Bartolina Sisa in El Alto; the first siege lasted 109 days, from March until June, and the city held out with troops sent from Buenos Aires.

By 5 August he besieged the city again, joined by Andrés Túpac Amaru; the siege was broken by royalist forces on 17 October 1781. Betrayed by some of his followers, he was captured on the night of 9 November and executed by quartering. His reported last words were 'I die but will return tomorrow as thousand thousands'. Bartolina Sisa and Gregoria Apaza were also executed. In 2005 Bolivia declared Julián Apaza and Bartolina Sisa national Aymara heroes.

coro-rebellion-1795.summary: In 1795 the free zambo José Leonardo Chirino, who had been to Saint-Domingue, led a rising at Coro for a republic, the freedom of all enslaved Africans and the end of native tribute; it was crushed, his children were sold into slavery, and he was executed in December 1796.

Its four aims were an independent democratic republic without monarchy or colonialism, the freedom of all enslaved Africans and the abolition of slavery, the abolition of the tribute imposed on the indigenous population, and the abolition of privilege and prejudice by skin colour. After the rising was suppressed Chirino was betrayed by an associate and condemned to death; his children were sold into slavery, and he was executed on December 10, 1796.

fedons-rebellion-grenada-1795-1796.summary: From March 1795 to June 1796 the free coloured planter Julien Fédon led a revolutionary army in Grenada, inspired by the French Revolution and the Haitian Revolution, that aimed to found a Black republic; the British under General Ralph Abercromby eventually crushed the rebellion, in which some 7,000 people were killed.
account: On 2 March 1795 Julien Fédon, a free coloured plantation owner who took the title "General-in-chief of the Grenadian rebel army," launched a rebellion against British rule in Grenada. The rebels, inspired by the French Revolution, the Haitian Revolution and Thomas Paine's Rights of Man, wore tricolour sashes and used the slogan "liberty, equality or death"; their goal was to found a Black republic as had already happened in neighbouring Haiti.

On 8 April 1795 Fédon's forces attacked Belvidere and took hostages, including the governor, Ninian Home; Fédon later had 44 of his 47 hostages killed. In the fighting the British lost 27 dead and 57 wounded at Belvidere alone, and the rebellion caused about £2,500,000 in damage to plantations and distilleries. General Ralph Abercromby's forces eventually defeated the rebellion on 19 June 1796; roughly 7,000 people were killed in the uprising, and Fédon himself disappeared, apparently drowning while trying to escape to Trinidad.

garifuna-deportation-1797.summary: After the Second Carib War the British deported the Black Caribs of Saint Vincent; more than 5,000 were deported and about 2,500 survived to land on Roatán in Honduras on April 12, 1797, founding the Garifuna of Central America.
account: The Garifuna descend from Indigenous Arawak and Kalinago people and Afro-Caribbean people. On Saint Vincent, which Britain took in 1763, the Black Caribs fought the First Carib War and, from March 1795, the Second; their chief Joseph Chatoyer was killed on 14 March 1795, and the Caribs surrendered in 1796.

In 1797 the British chose the Caribs with African features for deportation, as the supposed cause of the revolt, while those with more Amerindian traits were allowed to stay. More than 5,000 Black Caribs were deported, first toward Jamaica and then to Roatán, but when they landed on Roatán on April 12, 1797 only about 2,500 had survived. From Honduras they spread along the Caribbean coast to Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, where they became known as the Garifuna.

second-maroon-war-trelawny-deportation-1.place: Trelawny Town, Jamaica; Nova Scotia; Sierra Leone
second-maroon-war-trelawny-deportation-1.summary: An eight-month war in 1795–1796 between the British and the Trelawny Town Maroons of Jamaica ended with Governor Lord Balcarres deporting about 581 Maroons to Nova Scotia despite the British commander's earlier promise against transportation; after a harsh winter there, the Maroons petitioned to move on and resettled in the new colony of Sierra Leone by the start of the nineteenth century.
account: The Second Maroon War lasted about eight months in 1795–1796, pitting the British colonial government against the Trelawny Town Maroons under leaders including Montague James, John Jarrett, Leonard Parkinson and James Palmer. The British commander, General George Walpole, had assured the Maroons they would not be deported if they surrendered, but Governor Lord Balcarres used a minor delay in the peace terms as grounds to deport them anyway; Walpole resigned in protest and complained in Parliament, without success.

In 1796 about 581 Trelawny Maroons were shipped to Nova Scotia, while 58 others stayed behind in Jamaica. Seventeen died during the crossing, and another 19 died in the harsh winter of 1796–1797 while 5 were born, leaving about 550 by 1797. Unhappy in Nova Scotia, the Maroons asked to be moved again, and relocated to the new British settlement of Freetown, Sierra Leone, at the start of the nineteenth century.

haiti-declares-independence-1804.summary: On January 1, 1804, at Gonaïves, Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independence of Haiti, ending thirteen years of revolution and founding the first state in the world born of a successful uprising of enslaved people.
account: Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed Haitian independence on January 1, 1804, in the port city of Gonaïves, concluding the Haitian Revolution that had begun in 1791. Dessalines, himself formerly enslaved and unable to write French, had his secretary Louis Boisrond-Tonnerre compose and read the declaration; seventeen senior military officers signed it. Haiti became the first independent nation of Latin America and the Caribbean and the second in the Americas after the United States, and the first state founded by formerly enslaved people to abolish slavery outright.

The declaration emphasized emancipation and retribution against the French colonizers rather than the civic language of other independence documents of the era. Only two original printed copies of the declaration are known to survive; both were found in the UK National Archives between 2010 and 2011 by historian Julia Gaffield.

tecumseh-confederacy-1805-1813.place: Prophetstown (Tippecanoe), Indiana, to the Thames, Upper Canada
tecumseh-confederacy-1805-1813.summary: From 1805 the Shawnee prophet Tenskwatawa and his brother Tecumseh gathered thousands of Native people at Prophetstown into a confederacy against American expansion; it was attacked at Tippecanoe in 1811 and broke apart when Tecumseh was killed at the Thames in 1813.
account: Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet”, emerged in 1805 as the leader of a religious revival, and his brother Tecumseh led the confederation from as early as 1808. Their village of Prophetstown, near the meeting of the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers, became the largest Native community in the Great Lakes region; thousands gathered there for spiritual strength, and it stood for a time as a barrier to settlers moving west.

In November 1811 a US Army force under William Henry Harrison defeated warriors associated with Tenskwatawa at the Battle of Tippecanoe. Tecumseh then led the confederation, allied with the British, into war with the United States as part of the War of 1812. He was killed at the Battle of the Thames in Upper Canada on October 5, 1813, and the confederacy collapsed.

He was shown that the European invaders from the east were the children of the evil spirit, and told his people not to follow the white man or his customs.

dessalines-assassination-1806.summary: Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who had led Haiti's independence in 1804 and declared himself Emperor, was ambushed and killed on October 17, 1806 by a conspiracy of his own officers, including Alexandre Pétion, after his land-redistribution and forced-labor policies turned the new elite and the formerly enslaved population against him.
account: After declaring Haiti's independence in 1804, Jean-Jacques Dessalines ruled as Emperor Jacques I and enforced a plantation-labor system to rebuild the devastated economy, a policy the newly freed population experienced as a return to the conditions of slavery. His land-redistribution plans also alienated the mixed-race landowning elite, and senior military officers grew to resent his autocratic rule.

Disaffected officers under his own command, including Alexandre Pétion and Étienne-Élie Gérin, organized a conspiracy against him. On October 17, 1806, Dessalines was ambushed at Pont-Rouge (then called Larnage), just north of Port-au-Prince, and killed; accounts differ on whether he was shot, stabbed, or struck with a sabre, but his body was reportedly dismembered by a mob afterward. A woman named Dédée Bazile gathered his remains and arranged his burial at the Church of Sainte-Anne.

Dessalines's death split Haiti into a northern kingdom under Henri Christophe and a southern republic under Pétion, a division that lasted until Christophe's successor was overthrown and Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified the country in 1820.

Afro-Mexicans such as Vicente Guerrero and José María Morelos played crucial roles in the independence movement; Guerrero's terms were total independence and citizenship without caste distinction.

aponte-conspiracy-1812.place: Havana, Puerto Príncipe (Camagüey), Bayamo and Holguín, Cuba
aponte-conspiracy-1812.summary: In 1811–1812 the free black carpenter and militia corporal José Antonio Aponte of Havana organized an island-wide conspiracy to end slavery in Cuba; it was crushed, and Aponte was hanged on 9 April 1812, his head displayed in an iron cage.
account: As slavery expanded in Cuba at the beginning of the 19th century to take Haiti's place as the major sugar producer, a series of conspiracies against it followed; the first was discovered at Bayamo in 1795, headed by the freedman Nicolás Morales. In 1811 in Havana a new abolitionist conspiracy was organized by the freedman José Antonio Aponte, a first corporal in Havana's black militia of Yoruba origin, with reach to Sancti Spíritus, Trinidad, Camagüey, Bayamo, Holguín and Santiago. Hilario Herrera, a Dominican, tied the western conspiracy to the east.

The movement struck several sugar plantations outside Havana in March 1812 but was soon crushed. In Holguín more than 50 people were apprehended and the local leader, Juan Nepomuceno, from the Congo, was hanged. Hundreds of the enslaved were arrested and many leaders were tried and executed.

Aponte, convicted with eight of his companions on the evidence of his book of drawings, was hanged on 9 April 1812; he was then decapitated, his head placed in an iron cage in front of the house where he lived and his hand displayed on another street.

kingdom-of-haiti-christophe-1811.summary: After Haiti split following Dessalines's 1806 assassination, Henri Christophe ruled the north, proclaiming himself King Henry I on 28 March 1811 and building the Citadelle Laferrière and the Sans-Souci Palace before his death in 1820 ended the kingdom.
account: Following the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806, Haiti split between a northern state under Henri Christophe and a southern republic led by Alexandre Pétion. Christophe proclaimed the Kingdom of Haiti on 28 March 1811 and was crowned King Henry I on 2 June 1811.

Christophe's government organized agricultural workers under a military-style system of forced labour, caporalisme agraire, to keep sugar and coffee exports running. He used this labour, along with the kingdom's resources, to build six castles, eight palaces including the Sans-Souci Palace (largely completed by 1813), the Royal Chapel of Milot, and the Citadelle Laferrière, a mountaintop fortress built to defend the north against a feared French invasion to restore slavery.

Christophe suffered a stroke in August 1820 and, facing an uprising, shot himself at the Citadelle on 8 October 1820. His son and heir, Jacques-Victor Henry, was proclaimed king but was hanged by the insurgents ten days later, on 18 October 1820; Jean-Pierre Boyer, who had succeeded Pétion as president of the south in 1818, then reunified the country.

Forty years later, in 1853, the constitution abolished slavery completely; universities did not admit Black people until then. Black men served in the Regimiento de Pardos y Morenos, which gained regimental status in 1810 and fought in the war of independence.

creek-war-and-horseshoe-bend-1814.summary: Andrew Jackson’s army crushed the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend on March 27, 1814, killing at least 800 of about 1,000 warriors; the Treaty of Fort Jackson then forced the Creek Nation to give up more than 21 million acres.
account: The Red Sticks, a Muscogee faction resisting US expansion, attacked Fort Mims on August 30, 1813. On March 27, 1814 Jackson’s troops with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies stormed the Red Stick camp at Tohopeka on the Tallapoosa River. The National Park Service counts at least 800 of Chief Menawa’s 1,000 Red Sticks dead, 557 on the field and 200–300 in the river; Jackson lost 49 killed. Afterwards Jackson’s troops cut bridle reins from the skin of the dead and counted bodies by cutting off the tips of their noses.

The wounded Menawa led about 20 survivors across the river to join the Seminole in Spanish Florida. In August 1814 the Treaty of Fort Jackson ended the war and forced the Creek confederacy to surrender its land in what is now southern Georgia and central Alabama; Alabama was carved from it and admitted in 1819.

points: The Native Americans resisted Anglo-American encroachment on their lands after 1800 as best they could, in the Creek wars of 1813 and 1836 and the wars with the Seminoles that lasted into the 1850s: they fought hard and had much integrity. The southeastern nations who tried to imitate the whites, taking up private land and slaves, were called “civilized” for it.

royal-decree-of-graces-1815.summary: On 10 August 1815 Ferdinand VII granted free land and incentives to Spaniards and other Catholic Europeans to settle Puerto Rico, to build a loyal population and a plantation economy worked by enslaved Africans and poor jornaleros; it 'whitened' the island into the 1850s.
account: On 10 August 1815 King Ferdinand VII approved a royal decree of graces opening Puerto Rico to trade with countries in good standing with Spain and granting free land and incentives to Spaniards willing to settle. An earlier decree of 1789 had granted Spanish subjects the right to purchase slaves and to take part in the transatlantic slave trade.

By 1825 Spain had lost all its American possessions but Puerto Rico and Cuba. Fearing the native-born mixed-race criollos would follow Haiti and the mainland into independence, the Crown revived the decree and distributed it across Europe to attract settlers who would be more loyal, on condition of loyalty to the Crown and allegiance to the Roman Catholic Church. Corsicans, Italians, French, Portuguese, Irish, Scots, Germans and others came from 1830 onward.

The settlers built sugarcane, coffee and tobacco plantations on enslaved African labour and needy jornaleros. The decree attracted many European immigrants, in effect 'whitening' the island into the 1850s; heavy immigration swelled the population to about one million by the end of the century, decreasing the proportion of Africans. Spain abolished the slave trade to its colonies on 25 June 1835, but slavery was not abolished in Puerto Rico until 1873.

negro-fort-1816.summary: On July 27, 1816 a US force sent on Andrew Jackson’s orders destroyed the Negro Fort on the Apalachicola, a stronghold of free Black people and their Native allies in Spanish Florida, when a heated cannonball struck its powder magazine.
account: The British built the fort at Prospect Bluff in 1814 during the War of 1812 and left its arms behind. Fugitive slaves had sought refuge in Florida for generations, received by the Seminoles; the settlement at the fort became “the largest concentration of refugees from chattel slavery in the South between the end of the Revolution and the Civil War”, a Black Seminole stronghold under the command of Garçon, a former slave from Pensacola.

Jackson ordered General Gaines to destroy it and “return the stolen negroes and property to their rightful owners.” Garçon refused to surrender and raised a red flag of no quarter. On July 27, 1816 a heated cannonball landed in the magazine and the explosion was heard more than 100 miles away; almost every source says all but about 60 of the 334 occupants were killed at once, many of them women and children. Garçon and a Choctaw chief, among the few survivors, were handed to the Creek allies, who shot Garçon and scalped the chief.

British forces lost only one soldier and one civilian. Of the rebels, 50 were killed in the fighting, including Bussa, while the revolt continued briefly under his surviving forces; afterward colonial authorities executed 214 more enslaved people, exiled 170, and mutilated many others. It was the largest slave revolt in Barbadian history and the first of three major revolts (with the Demerara rebellion of 1823 and Jamaica's Baptist War of 1831–1832) that helped push Britain toward abolition.

bolivar-petion-and-abolition-in-gran-col.summary: In 1816 Simón Bolívar won arms and money from Haiti's president Alexandre Pétion by pledging to free the slaves of the lands he took; yet the republics freed only the newborn at first, and slavery lasted until 1851 in Colombia and Ecuador, 1854 in Venezuela and Peru, and 1869 in Paraguay.
account: Forced into exile on Jamaica after Spanish forces subdued New Granada in 1815, Bolívar reached Les Cayes in Haiti on 24 December and met Pétion on 2 January 1816; after he pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, Pétion gave him money and military supplies. Realising the importance of Black soldiers, Bolívar declared the abolition of slavery in 1812 and again in 1816.

After independence, the Congress of Cúcuta (1821) passed a law of free womb, manumission and abolition of the slave trade for what is now Colombia and Venezuela. Slavery was finally abolished in Colombia in 1851 and in Ecuador in 1851; in Venezuela on 24 March 1854, when fewer than 24,000 slaves remained; and in Peru in 1854 by President Ramón Castilla. Paraguay adopted a free womb law in 1842 and abolished slavery for all ages in 1869.

central-american-independence-and-abolit.summary: Central America declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821 and, after a brief union with Mexico, formed the Federal Republic of Central America, which abolished slavery by federal decree on 17 April 1824.
account: The provinces of Central America became independent of the Spanish Empire on 15 September 1821 and of the First Mexican Empire on 1 July 1823. The Federal Republic of Central America, joining Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, adopted its constitution on 22 November 1824; it had 1,287,491 people in 1824 and dissolved in 1839.

Slavery was abolished on 17 April 1824 by federal decree. Indigenous slaves had built and maintained Central America's roads, and their construction and upkeep nearly ended with abolition. Indigenous tribute had been abolished in 1811; in El Salvador in 1833 the Indigenous laborer Anastasio Aquino led 2,000 followers in rebellion after killings of Indigenous people, and was executed that July.

puerto-rico-slave-revolts-and-prims-blac.summary: As sugar and slavery grew in 19th-century Puerto Rico, the enslaved conspired and revolted more than twenty times; in 1821 Marcos Xiorro planned a revolt against the planters, and on 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim imposed the Bando contra la Raza Africana to control all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved.
account: In the 19th century Spain established and expanded sugar cane production in Puerto Rico, and slavery increased. By 1873 the enslaved had carried out more than twenty revolts, some of great political importance, such as the Ponce and Vega Baja conspiracies.

In July 1821 the enslaved Marcos Xiorro planned and conspired to lead a revolt against the sugar planters and the Spanish colonial government. The conspiracy was suppressed, but Xiorro achieved legendary status among the enslaved and is part of Puerto Rico's heroic folklore.

Planters, nervous at the number of the enslaved, ordered restrictions on their movement; black Puerto Ricans were made to carry a notebook, the libreta, to move around the island. On 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim, fearing an independence or slave revolt, imposed draconian laws, the Bando contra la Raza Africana, to control the behaviour of all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved. Juan de la Pezuela replaced Prim that same year. In the Grito de Lares of 1868, free blacks who resented the libreta system burned their notebooks.

pichincha-and-ayacucho-1822-1824.summary: Bolívar's general Antonio José de Sucre defeated the royalists on the slopes of Pichincha above Quito on May 24, 1822 and at Ayacucho on December 9, 1824, securing the independence of Ecuador within Gran Colombia and of Peru, and ending the Spanish American wars of independence.
account: Guayaquil proclaimed its independence on October 9, 1820. Sucre, Bolívar's most trusted subordinate, took command of a patriot army there, and on 24 May 1822, on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano 3,500 metres above sea level beside Quito, defeated the royalist army of Melchor Aymerich, liberating Quito and the provinces of its Audiencia, from which Ecuador would emerge. Gran Colombia was dissolved in 1831.

On 9 December 1824 Sucre's independentist army met the royalists at Pampa de Ayacucho near Quinua; Viceroy José de la Serna was wounded, and his second in command signed the capitulation of the royalist army. The battle secured the independence of Peru and is considered in Peru the end of the Spanish American wars of independence.

Invading from Colombia in 1822, the armies of Simón Bolívar and Sucre came to the aid of the Ecuadorian rebels, and on May 24 Sucre won at Pichincha. Bolívar fought the Spanish dependency created when they came over; but those born of Spain in these countries fought against him, and they could not unify.

haitian-unification-hispaniola-1822.place: Santo Domingo and all of Hispaniola
haitian-unification-hispaniola-1822.summary: President Jean-Pierre Boyer, who had reunified Haiti in 1820, marched an army of 12,000 into the newly independent Republic of Spanish Haiti and entered Santo Domingo on 9 February 1822, ruling the whole island until Dominican nationalists broke away on 27 February 1844.
account: Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified Haiti's north and south in 1820 after Henri Christophe's death. When the Spanish-speaking east briefly declared itself the independent Republic of Spanish Haiti in late 1821, Boyer marched in with 12,000 soldiers in February 1822 and formally entered Santo Domingo on 9 February 1822, unifying the whole island of Hispaniola under Haitian rule for the next twenty-two years.

Boyer's government forbade white elites from owning land and forcibly stripped major Dominican landowning families of their property; it tried and largely failed to force the export-crop production of the 1826 and 1838 Code Rural on the east, and to pay France's 150-million-franc independence indemnity it imposed heavy taxation and let occupying soldiers commandeer food and supplies by force, reducing Dominicans to a position the Code Rural had already made of Haiti's own peasantry.

Boyer lost the support of the Haitian elite and was ousted in 1843, replaced by Charles Rivière-Hérard. On 27 February 1844 Dominican nationalists led by Juan Pablo Duarte and the secret society La Trinitaria seized Santo Domingo and declared the independent Dominican Republic, ending the twenty-two-year unification.

demerara-rebellion-1823.summary: On 18–20 August 1823 between 9,000 and 15,000 enslaved people across some 37 plantations in Demerara, British Guiana, rose up under Jack Gladstone and his father Quamina after wrongly believing Parliament had already freed them; colonial forces killed hundreds suppressing the revolt, executed 27 rebels, killed Quamina and left his body on a gibbet, and the death in prison of the missionary John Smith, convicted alongside them, galvanised British abolitionists.
account: On 18–20 August 1823, between 9,000 and 15,000 enslaved people across about 37 estates on Demerara's east coast rose up, led by Jack Gladstone, an enslaved man on the Success plantation, and his father Quamina, along with other members of their church. The revolt was triggered by a mistaken belief that Parliament in London had already abolished slavery, combined with harsh plantation conditions and religious restrictions.

Colonial forces under Governor John Murray suppressed the rising, killing between 200 and 500 enslaved people; bodies were left on public display for months as a warning. Twenty-seven rebels were executed, out of 45 death sentences handed down. Jack Gladstone was captured on 6 September and deported, probably to Saint Lucia; Quamina was killed by trackers and his body was hung on a gibbet. The English Congregationalist missionary John Smith, tried alongside the rebels and sentenced to death, died in prison awaiting the outcome of his appeal; his case became a rallying point for the British abolitionist movement in the years before the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.

marshall-court-indian-cases-1823-1832.place: Washington, D.C.; the Cherokee Nation, Georgia
marshall-court-indian-cases-1823-1832.summary: In three cases Chief Justice John Marshall’s court laid down the doctrine of discovery (1823), called the Cherokee a “domestic dependent nation” (1831), and upheld Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia (1832), a ruling that did not save them from removal.
account: In Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823) Marshall set out the “discovery doctrine”: a European power gains sovereignty over the land it discovers and the exclusive right to extinguish the Native occupants’ “right of occupancy”. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (March 18, 1831) he held that the Cherokee Nation was not a foreign nation but a “domestic dependent nation”, its relation to the United States like that of “a ward to its guardian”.

In Worcester v. Georgia (March 3, 1832) the Court struck down Georgia’s law barring non-Natives from Cherokee land without a state license, building the foundations of tribal sovereignty. Jackson wrote that the decision “has fell still born”; the words “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it!” are believed to be apocryphal. On December 29, 1835 a few Cherokees without authority signed the removal Treaty of New Echota; Justice Stephen Breyer later observed that the Cherokee nation was the “obvious loser”.

date.text: April 17, 1825 ordinance; reduced February 12, 1838; last indemnity payment 1883; final related debt retired 1947

french-indemnity-haiti-1825.summary: On April 17, 1825, French King Charles X, backing his demand with fourteen warships, ordered Haiti to pay 150 million francs as compensation to former French slaveholders in exchange for recognizing its independence; the debt and the loans taken to pay it burdened Haiti's economy for over a century.
account: On April 17, 1825, Charles X issued an ordinance demanding Haiti pay 150 million francs in five annual installments of 30 million, as compensation for the property, including enslaved people, that French colonists had lost in the Haitian Revolution, and requiring Haiti to halve its import duties for French merchants. France delivered the ultimatum by force: Baron de Mackau arrived at Port-au-Prince on July 3, 1825, aboard the warship La Circe, and a fleet eventually totaling fourteen French warships carrying 528 cannons backed the demand. President Jean-Pierre Boyer accepted the terms rather than risk invasion and the restoration of slavery.

Haiti could not pay from its own revenue and borrowed from French banks to make the first payments, compounding the debt with interest -- commonly called Haiti's "double debt." On February 12, 1838, France reduced the remaining balance to 90 million francs, payable over 30 years. Haiti made its last indemnity remittance in 1883, but loans taken to service that debt were not fully repaid, to the National City Bank of New York, until 1947. A 2022 New York Times analysis estimated the debt and its associated loans removed between $21 billion and $115 billion of economic growth from Haiti over two centuries.

mexico-abolishes-slavery-1829.summary: On 16 September 1829 the government of Vicente Guerrero, Mexico's first president of African ancestry, proclaimed the abolition of slavery across almost all the nation; under pressure from Texan settlers he exempted Texas that December.
account: The slave trade had been banned by the Spanish authorities in 1818, a ban confirmed by the Mexican government in 1824, and a few states had already abolished slavery. Guerrero, who became president on 1 April 1829, proclaimed abolition across almost all of Mexico on 16 September 1829. Slavery by then barely existed except in Coahuila y Tejas, where slave owners from the United States had settled; in response to pressure from Texan settlers Guerrero exempted Texas on 2 December 1829.

In 1830 Anglo-Texans evaded the law by declaring their slaves "indentured servants for life"; in 1832 at Anahuac a Mexican officer enforced abolition and refused to hand over two escaped slaves. Guerrero was overthrown and executed by firing squad at Cuilapan, Oaxaca, on 14 February 1831.

account: Turner interpreted the eclipse of February 12, 1831 and an atmospheric disturbance on August 13 as divine signals, and began the rebellion on Sunday, August 21. About 55 white people were killed. White mobs killed as many as 120 enslaved and free Black people in retaliation, and Virginia executed eighteen accused of taking part.

Turner was tried on November 5, 1831, convicted and hanged on November 11 at Jerusalem (now Courtland), Virginia; his body was dissected and flayed. Because Turner was educated and a preacher, Southern legislatures passed laws against teaching enslaved and free Black people and restricting their assembly.

baptist-war-jamaica-1831-1832.summary: Beginning on Christmas Day 1831 a Black Baptist deacon, Samuel Sharpe, led a rebellion that drew in up to 60,000 of Jamaica's roughly 300,000 enslaved people; colonial forces killed hundreds suppressing it and executed Sharpe and hundreds more afterward, and the scale of the reprisals helped push Parliament toward the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.
account: The Baptist War, also called the Christmas Rebellion, began on 25 December 1831 and lasted until 5 January 1832, led by Samuel Sharpe, a literate Black Baptist deacon who had organised a plan for a peaceful strike for wages and freedom that turned into an armed uprising. Up to 60,000 of Jamaica's roughly 300,000 enslaved people took part.

Fourteen white colonists were killed. At least 307 rebels were killed during the revolt, and colonial courts afterward executed another 310 to 340 enslaved Jamaicans, including Sharpe and the planter-militiaman Robert Gardner, for offences ranging from rebellion to minor property crimes. Property damage was assessed at £1,154,589. Though militarily defeated, the uprising's brutality and scale were widely reported in Britain and accelerated the passage of the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.

account: The Slavery Abolition Act received royal assent on 28 August 1833 and came into force on 1 August 1834. Enslaved people over the age of six became "apprentices" rather than being immediately freed outright; the first apprenticeships were due to end on 1 August 1838 and the rest on 1 August 1840, but most colonies ended the system early, with Jamaica the last to do so, in the middle of June 1838.

The British government paid £20 million — about 40% of the Treasury's entire annual income in 1833 — to compensate the roughly 800,000 enslaved people's owners for the loss of their human property; the formerly enslaved received no compensation. About 800,000 freed people were recorded in the compensation claims process across the British Caribbean.

The Court ordered their release; thirty-five survivors were returned to their homeland, the others having died at sea or in prison.

la-escalera-and-triunvirato-1843-1844.summary: After a series of slave revolts in 1843, led at the Triunvirato plantation by the Yoruba women Carlota and Fermina, the Spanish authorities claimed to uncover La Escalera, a conspiracy to end slavery, and answered with a terror in which thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished.
account: In March, May and November 1843 a series of slave revolts occurred in Cuba. On 5 November 1843 the enslaved of the Triunvirato sugar mill in Matanzas rose, led by the African-born Lucumí women Carlota and Fermina with Eduardo, Narciso and Felipe Lucumí and Manuel Gangá; the revolt spread to the neighbouring Acaná estate and reached five plantations. Fermina had been whipped and kept in iron shackles for five months for running away. Carlota died in battle at the end of the revolt.

In December 1843 an enslaved woman, Polonia Gangá, told her master his property was about to be overtaken, and the authorities turned to stopping what they called the Conspiración de La Escalera, an alleged plot to abolish slavery. The British consul David Turnbull, already expelled, was convicted in absentia as its 'prime mover'. Historians have debated whether the conspiracy was real; there now seems to be a consensus that some revolt was planned.

The repression is called the Year of the Lash (Año del Cuero). La Escalera, 'the ladder', alludes to suspects being bound to ladders and whipped during interrogation. Thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished; on 29 June 1844 a firing squad in Havana executed accused leaders. In 1912 Pedro Ivonnet of the Independent Party of Color called his party's exclusion "the epilogue of the trial of la Escalera."

account: The Caste War began in 1847 with the revolt of the Indigenous Maya of Yucatán against the Hispanic Yucatecos. After independence, Yucatecan laws had encouraged the taking of Maya communal land for henequen and sugar plantations, forcing many Maya to work as indebted laborers on haciendas. The Maya state of Chan Santa Cruz, trading with British Honduras (Belize), was recognized by Britain; Maya fleeing the war settled in British Honduras and the Petén. The Mexican army occupied Chan Santa Cruz in 1901, the formal end came in 1915, and the population of Yucatán was halved through war, disease or migration; the total dead is given as 364,000.

During the war the Yucatán government sold Maya prisoners into slavery, and the peninsula became a platform for the Cuban slave trade. The paddle steamer La Unión carried enslaved Maya from Mexico to Cuba from 1855 to 1861; in September 1861 she sank near Sisal when her boiler exploded. The wreck was found in 2017.

In May 2017 the governor of Coahuila recognized the “tribu de los negros mascogos” as an Indigenous people of the state.

In 2019 Governor Gavin Newsom called it a genocide and apologized for the violence sanctioned by the state.

occupation-of-araucania.summary: From 1861 to 1883 Chilean soldiers and settlers advanced into the Mapuche lands of Araucanía, independent through the whole colonial era, and incorporated them into Chile; thousands of Mapuche died by war and disease, chiefly smallpox, and their lands were reduced, plunging many into lasting poverty.

Economic and geopolitical reasons, with increasingly negative attitudes towards the Mapuche, led Chile to seek its incorporation by force if necessary. Colonel Cornelio Saavedra Rodríguez planned a state-led colonization influenced by the United States frontier; in 1861 he ordered Major Pedro Lagos to advance to the confluence of the Mulchén and Bureo rivers.

For ten years (1861–1871) the Mapuche could not stop the advance; the war brought famine in the winter of 1869, worsened by smallpox. After a decade of near peace, while Chile fought Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific, a large Chilean army reached the Cautín River in March 1881; a last coordinated Mapuche rising in November 1881 was defeated within days. The conflict killed thousands of Mapuche by warfare and disease, primarily smallpox, and the pillaging of the army and bandits and the reduction of their lands plunged many into poverty that has persisted for generations. It ran alongside Argentina's campaigns against the Mapuche of 1878–1885.
