black-codes-1865.summary: In 1865 and 1866 the legislatures of the former slave states passed Black Codes: laws that limited the freedom of the newly emancipated and forced them back into labor for white employers.
account: After chattel slavery was abolished throughout the United States in 1865, the former slave states of the South enacted Black Codes to restrict black citizens, especially the emancipated freedmen. Their defining feature was broad vagrancy laws, and they were particularly concerned with controlling the movement and labor of freedmen.

Mississippi was the first state to pass them. Its law allowed black people to rent land only within cities, required them to present written proof of employment each January, and made the lack of it vagrancy, punishable by arrest. South Carolina, Alabama and Louisiana followed in 1865, and Florida, Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina, Texas, Tennessee and Arkansas at the beginning of 1866.

The codes granted some limited rights, such as owning personal property and marrying, but black people were barred from testifying against white people and faced severe penalties for unemployment. Intense Northern reaction against the Mississippi and South Carolina laws led some later states to remove overt racial language, while keeping vagrancy and apprenticeship laws that worked to the same end.

forty-acres-and-the-freedmans-bank-1865.place: Sea Islands and coast of Georgia and South Carolina; Washington, D.C.
forty-acres-and-the-freedmans-bank-1865.summary: Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 set aside land in plots of up to 40 acres for freed families, but President Andrew Johnson reversed the policy in 1865; the Freedman's Savings Bank, chartered the same year, failed in 1874 with the savings of its depositors.
account: On January 16, 1865, General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15, instructing officers to settle freed refugees on the Sea Islands and inland: 400,000 acres divided into plots of no more than 40 acres. Mules were not mentioned in the order, though some beneficiaries received them from the army.

Freed people widely expected to claim 40 acres of land. In 1865 Abraham Lincoln's successor, Andrew Johnson, tried to reverse the intent of the order and of similar provisions in the second Freedmen's Bureau bills; as one of the first acts of Reconstruction he ordered all land under federal control returned to the owners from whom it had been seized.

The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company was chartered by Congress on March 3, 1865, to collect deposits from Black people, especially the formerly enslaved. It opened 37 branches in 17 states and Washington, D.C., and collected funds from over 67,000 depositors, holding more than $3.7 million at its height in 1872. Its growth rested on false claims, mismanagement and fraud: its white officials made speculative and insider loans, and its advertising implied a government guarantee it did not have.

In March 1874 the trustees deposed its president, John W. Alvord, and elected Frederick Douglass. The bank failed in 1874, destroying the savings of many African Americans and, historians believe, their trust in financial institutions.

convict-leasing.summary: Using the Thirteenth Amendment's exception for punishment of crime, Southern states leased prisoners, the great majority of them Black men convicted under the Black Codes and vagrancy laws, to planters and companies.
account: Louisiana leased out convicted people as early as 1844, and the system expanded throughout most of the South with emancipation in 1865. Its constitutional basis was the 1865 Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude “except as a punishment for crime”.

Black Codes, pig laws and vagrancy laws criminalized unemployment, homelessness and changes of employment, creating a new criminal class of freed people. By the 1880s Black people made up 80 to 90 percent of those incarcerated in the South.

The system was highly lucrative: in 1898, 73 percent of Alabama's annual state revenue came from convict leasing. The practice peaked about 1880 and was gradually phased out after Attorney General Francis Biddle's Circular No. 3591 of December 12, 1941. In February 2018 the remains of 95 people, victims of convict leasing, were unearthed on a former sugar plantation in Sugar Land, Texas.

date.text: Widespread from Reconstruction (1865–1877); declined from the late 1930s and 1940s

sharecropping.summary: After the Civil War most freed people, with no land, worked white-owned land for a share of the crop, bound by debt to the landowner or merchant.
account: Under sharecropping, landowners provided land, housing, tools and seed, and merchants supplied food on credit; at the end of the season the cropper paid the owner a share of the crop, typically one-half to two-thirds. If what was left came to less than what he owed, he remained in debt. Under the crop lien the planter or merchant took the year's crop as collateral and settled the debt when it was sold.

Sharecropping became widespread in the South during Reconstruction (1865–1877), after President Johnson returned the land set aside by Sherman's Field Order No. 15. In Mississippi by 1900, 85 percent of black farmers were tenants or sharecroppers. Around Elaine, Arkansas, landowners kept sharecroppers in debt through plantation-store prices and underpayment for crops, and it was an unwritten law that a sharecropper could not leave until his debts were paid.
Traditional sharecropping declined after farm mechanization became economical in the late 1930s and early 1940s, and many sharecroppers moved to the cities.

buffalo-soldiers-1866.summary: From 1866 the U.S. Army raised all-black regiments, later called the Buffalo Soldiers, who served on the frontier and fought in the Western Indian Wars.
account: Buffalo Soldiers were United States Army regiments composed exclusively of Black American soldiers, formed during the 19th century to serve on the American frontier. On September 21, 1866, the 10th Cavalry Regiment was formed at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Congress established them as the first all-black Army regiments in peacetime, and they were racially segregated.

They fought in the Western Indian Wars from 1867 to 1896, and also served in Cuba, the Philippines, Hawaii and Mexico. According to legend the name was given by the Apache and Cheyenne; 23 Buffalo Soldiers received the Medal of Honor during the Indian Wars.

In the 21st century their employment in the American Indian Wars has led some to call for a critical reappraisal of the regiments, seen by some as accessories to settler-colonial and westward expansion.

grito-de-lares-1868.place: Lares and San Sebastián del Pepino, Puerto Rico
grito-de-lares-1868.summary: On 23 September 1868 some 400–600 rebels of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico took Lares and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; the revolt was crushed within a day and hundreds were imprisoned.
account: Ramón Emeterio Betances and Segundo Ruiz Belvis founded the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico in exile in the Dominican Republic on 6 January 1868. Its cells, organized by Mathias Brugman, Mariana Bracetti and Manuel Rojas, brought together landowners, merchants, professionals, peasants and the enslaved; the economy, slavery and Spanish repression were the catalysts. Betances's arms ship was seized in Saint Thomas, and the plot was discovered in Camuy, so the leaders moved the date forward.

Some 400 to 600 rebels gathered at Manuel Rojas's estate and took Lares around midnight on 23 September 1868. In the church they placed the Lares flag on the altar and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico under Francisco Ramírez Medina, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; free blacks burned their libretas. The next morning the rebels were repulsed at San Sebastián del Pepino; four of them died.

Spanish forces arrested more than 800 suspects; some 475 rebels were imprisoned in Arecibo, where they were tortured and humiliated, and on 17 November a military court sentenced them all to death, though they were later amnestied. The revolt failed, but Spain granted more political autonomy. The Lares flag is recognized as the first flag of Puerto Rico.

reconstruction-amendments-1868-1870.summary: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made the freed people citizens with equal protection of the laws, and the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote on account of race, colour or previous servitude; within decades Southern states had stripped most black men of the vote again.
account: The Fourteenth Amendment was adopted on July 9, 1868, as one of the Reconstruction Amendments, a response to issues affecting freed slaves after the Civil War. Its Citizenship Clause superseded Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), which had held that Americans descended from African slaves could not become citizens.

The Fifteenth Amendment prohibits the federal government or any state from denying or abridging a citizen's right to vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." It was ratified on February 3, 1870, the third and last of the Reconstruction Amendments; no Democrat in either house voted for it.

Late nineteenth-century Supreme Court decisions read the amendment narrowly, and from 1890 to 1910 Southern Democrats adopted new state constitutions and Jim Crow laws that raised barriers to voter registration, removing most black voters from the rolls.

opelousas-and-colfax-massacres-1868-1873.summary: Two of the bloodiest massacres of Reconstruction struck black Republicans in Louisiana: at Opelousas in 1868 and at the Colfax courthouse on Easter Sunday 1873.
account: The Opelousas massacre in St. Landry Parish began on September 28, 1868, as tensions rose between white Democrats and Black Republicans after Louisiana's 1868 constitution gave Black men the vote. The white supremacist Knights of the White Camelia was thought to have 3,000 members in the parish. Estimates of the dead vary widely: Democratic papers reported 100 or fewer, Republicans 200 to 300, and other estimates 150 to 300 Black people and 30 to 50 whites.

On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, after the contested 1872 election, armed white men with rifles and a small cannon overpowered the Black freedmen and state militia holding the Grant Parish courthouse in Colfax. Between 62 and 153 Black men were murdered while surrendering, nearly another 50 of them later that night after being held prisoner. Many bodies were thrown into the Red River.

The federal convictions of a few perpetrators were appealed, and in United States v. Cruikshank (1876) the Supreme Court ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment's protections did not apply to individuals acting privately, ending federal prosecution of paramilitary groups such as the White League under the Enforcement Act of 1870.

ten-years-war-and-baragua-1868-1878.summary: On 10 October 1868 Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves and proclaimed Cuba's independence, beginning a ten-year war; at its end Antonio Maceo refused, in the Protest of Baraguá, a peace that neither freed Cuba nor abolished slavery.
account: In the early morning of 10 October 1868 the sugar-mill owner Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the cry of independence at La Demajagua, freed his slaves and asked them to join the struggle, calling on men of all races to fight. It was the first of Cuba's three wars of liberation against Spain. Céspedes was killed by a Spanish patrol on 27 February 1874. Spain sent more troops after 1876, until they numbered more than 250,000.

The Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878 ended most of the fighting; its most significant reform was freedom for the enslaved who had fought on either side. Antonio Maceo and other Mambises met General Martínez Campos at Los Mangos de Baraguá on 15 March 1878 and rejected it, because it won neither independence nor the abolition of slavery. Maceo fled to Jamaica in May, and hostilities ended on 28 May 1878.
Losses are estimated at 50,000 dead on the Cuban side and 81,248 Spanish dead, 75,000 of them from disease.

He was collector of the port of Beaufort from 1897 to 1913 and died there on February 23, 1915.

moret-law-1870.summary: The Moret Law of 4 July 1870 freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, the elderly and those who served Spain, beginning a gradual abolition in Cuba and Puerto Rico while owners were compensated.
account: After the U.S. Civil War, international pressure pushed Spain to end slavery in its last American colonies. The Moret Law, named after Segismundo Moret, Spain's Minister of Overseas Territories, was approved on 4 July 1870 for Cuba and later Puerto Rico; Spain also passed it hoping to preempt the independence movements.

It freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, and children under 14 were not to be separated from their mothers. It also freed the enslaved who served in the Spanish army, those over 60 and those owned by the government. The Spanish government compensated owners 125 pesetas for each person freed. Slavery was abolished in Puerto Rico, but not in Cuba, in 1873, and without exceptions in 1886.

account: In 1870 the Army asked John Horse to bring his band back to enlist as Indian scouts, promising them repatriation to Indian Territory. Most were moved to Fort Clark near Brackettville in July 1872, led by Lieutenant John L. Bullis. Adam Payne received the Medal of Honor for his courage against the Kiowas, and in 1875 John Ward, Isaac Payne and Pompey Factor received it for saving Bullis under fire. The scouts were disbanded in 1914 and most were forced to leave the Fort Clark reservation with their families.

Congress answered with what the Sioux call the “sell or starve” rider, cutting off all rations until they ceded the Black Hills, and the Act of February 28, 1877 removed the Black Hills from the reservation. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled that “a more ripe and rank case of dishonorable dealings will never, in all probability, be found in our history” and ordered compensation; the Sioux refused the money, which was worth over $1 billion by 2011, seeking the return of the land.

compromise-of-1877-and-jim-crow-laws.summary: The Compromise of 1877 ended federal military oversight of the South, and white-dominated legislatures enacted Jim Crow laws that segregated public life and took the vote from black citizens into the mid-20th century.
account: The Compromise of 1877 was an informal deal that settled the disputed 1876 presidential election: Democrats ended their filibuster of the certified results in exchange for the Republicans' ending military oversight of the South. When Rutherford B. Hayes took office he withdrew the last federal troops from the South, which historians largely regard as the end of Reconstruction. No written evidence of such a deal has ever been found.

The Jim Crow laws were state and local laws introduced in the Southern United States from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century that enforced racial segregation. They were enacted by white-dominated legislatures (Redeemers) to disenfranchise and remove the political and economic gains made by African Americans during Reconstruction, and were upheld in 1896 in Plessy v. Ferguson.
Facilities for African Americans were consistently inferior and underfunded, and companion laws excluded most African Americans from the vote in the South.

account: From 1885 to 1908 many atrocities were committed in the Congo Free State under the absolute rule of King Leopold II of Belgium, particularly associated with the labour policies used to collect natural rubber for export. cuban-war-of-independence-and-reconcentr.summary: Cuba's last war against Spain began on 24 February 1895; to cut the rebels off from the people, General Valeriano Weyler forced the rural population into fortified towns, where at least 170,000 Cubans, about one in ten, died of disease and hunger.
account: The insurrection organized by José Martí and Máximo Gómez began on 24 February 1895. Martí was killed soon after landing, on 19 May 1895 at Dos Ríos, but Gómez and Antonio Maceo carried the war across the island, reaching its western tip on 22 January 1896. Maceo, the 'Bronze Titan', was killed on 7 December 1896 in Havana province. Spain sent 220,285 soldiers to Cuba, the largest army to cross the Atlantic until World War II.

General Valeriano Weyler answered with periodic executions, mass exile, the destruction of farms and crops, and the reconcentration policy: rural Cubans had eight days to move into camps in fortified towns, and all who failed to obey were to be shot. Housing was decaying, food scarce and disease spread; by 1898 a third of the population had been moved into the camps. Historian John Lawrence Tone estimates that 155,000 to 170,000 civilians died, nearly 10% of the population; the policy is remembered as the first construction of modern concentration camps.
Weyler was dismissed in 1897 after the assassination of Prime Minister Cánovas; the policy was kept until March 1898. The final months of the war became the Spanish–American War.

foraker-act-and-insular-cases-1900-1901.summary: The Foraker Act of 12 April 1900 gave Puerto Rico a civil government whose governor, executive council and judges were appointed in Washington; in 1901 the Supreme Court's Insular Cases held that the Constitution did not fully apply there, calling the islands' peoples 'alien races'.
account: The Foraker Act, signed by President McKinley on 12 April 1900 and effective 1 May, replaced military rule with a civil government: a governor and an 11-member Executive Council appointed by the U.S. President, a 35-member elected House of Delegates, judges appointed by the President, and a non-voting Resident Commissioner in Congress. Congress could annul any law the island passed. It created a Puerto Rican citizenship and imposed tariffs on goods shipped to the United States.

In six opinions decided on 27 May 1901, among them Downes v. Bidwell, the Supreme Court held that full constitutional protection does not automatically extend to all places under American control, so that the people of unincorporated territories such as Puerto Rico, even if U.S. citizens, may lack some constitutional rights. Downes called the people of the insular areas 'alien races', and DeLima v. Bidwell termed them 'savage tribes'; the cases are widely considered racist.

platt-amendment-and-guantanamo-1901-1903.summary: As the price of withdrawing its troops, the United States made Cuba write into its constitution, and then into a 1903 treaty, a U.S. right to intervene in Cuban affairs and a lease of land for naval bases, which the U.S. still holds at Guantánamo Bay.
account: The Platt Amendment, part of the Army Appropriations Act signed by President McKinley on 2 March 1901, set seven conditions for the withdrawal of U.S. troops remaining in Cuba and an eighth that Cuba sign a treaty accepting them. Cuba amended its constitution to contain the seven demands word for word.

Its third article gave the United States the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence and a government adequate for the protection of life, property and individual liberty; another required Cuba to sell or lease land for coaling and naval stations. After U.S. troops withdrew in 1902, Cuba signed the Cuban–American Treaty of Relations on 22 May 1903 and leased land at Guantánamo Bay, which the U.S. still controls. The treaty was used to justify the second occupation of Cuba in 1906; in 1934 a new treaty dropped three of the seven pledges.
In 1912 the Independent Party of Color appealed to the third article for protection against the Cuban government's forces; the United States did not accept the plea.

independent-party-of-color-massacre-1912.place: Oriente and Las Villas provinces, Cuba
independent-party-of-color-massacre-1912.summary: Black veterans of the independence war founded the Partido Independiente de Color in 1908; banned under the Morúa law, it rose in Oriente in May 1912 and was crushed by the Cuban army with U.S. Marines guarding American property, with estimates of up to 6,000 dead.
account: The Partido Independiente de Color (PIC) was founded on 7 August 1908 by black and mixed-race veterans of the War of Independence, after no black politician was elected in the elections of 1 August 1908. Its platform called for equal treatment regardless of race, free university education, guaranteed public employment and land for veterans. It is described as the first black political party in the Western Hemisphere. Since the war, U.S. businesses had been taking up land in Oriente, where most Afro-Cubans lived.

President José Miguel Gómez had the party outlawed under the Morúa law, which banned parties based on race. The PIC petitioned President Taft under the Platt Amendment against "outrages against our persons and our rights"; the U.S. refused. Newspapers such as El Día cast the movement as a racist uprising of blacks.

On 20 May 1912 the rebels attacked the Cuban Army, mainly in Oriente. The government met them with severe repression and appealed to the United States, whose Marines moved to protect U.S.-owned property, railroads and mines. Evaristo Estenoz was killed on 27 June. Rebel forces had numbered at least 3,000; by June about 1,800 were left alive, and some sources cite as many as 6,000 deaths including civilians. Many Afro-Cubans were killed whether or not they were involved, and the party was disbanded. Pedro Ivonnet called the party's exclusion "the epilogue of the trial of la Escalera."

british-west-indies-regiment-taranto-mut.place: Palestine, France, Flanders, Italy; Taranto, Italy
british-west-indies-regiment-taranto-mut.summary: Some 15,600 West Indian volunteers served in the British West Indies Regiment in the First World War, mostly in Palestine, while being denied the pay and promotions given white soldiers; in December 1918, after the armistice, battalions gathered at Taranto, Italy mutinied over the discrimination, leading to disbandment, courts martial and one execution, but also to the founding of the Caribbean League, which demanded self-determination for the West Indies.
account: The British West Indies Regiment formed in 1915, its 1st Battalion mustering at Seaford, Sussex, on 1 October 1915 with recruits from Jamaica (about two-thirds of the roughly 15,600 men who served), British Guiana, Trinidad, Barbados, the Bahamas, British Honduras, the Leeward Islands, Saint Lucia and St Vincent. The regiment served mainly against Ottoman forces in Palestine and Jordan, with some battalions in France, Flanders and Italy; 262 men died, 105 of them in combat and 157 of disease, and 573 were wounded, while the regiment earned 81 medals for bravery and 49 mentions in despatches.

After the armistice, BWIR battalions gathered at Taranto, Italy to demobilise. Resentment grew when the men discovered white soldiers had received pay rises they were denied, despite being made to do menial labour — loading ships, fatigue duty and latrine work. On 6 December 1918 the 9th Battalion refused orders and 180 sergeants petitioned against the unequal pay and promotions; the 10th Battalion also refused work on 9 December. Over four days a Black NCO was killed and an officer assaulted before the Worcestershire Regiment restored order. The 9th Battalion was disbanded, about 60 men were court-martialled for mutiny and given sentences of three to five years (one got 20 years, and one was executed). On 17 December 1918 about 60 NCOs formed the Caribbean League, demanding equal rights and self-determination for the West Indies.

us-occupation-dominican-republic-1916.summary: US Marines occupied the Dominican Republic from May 15, 1916 to September 18, 1924, to force repayment of debts to European and American creditors, installing a military government that controlled Dominican finances through the National City Bank of New York while a guerrilla movement, the gavilleros, resisted in the eastern provinces.
account: After a 1916 power struggle between President Juan Isidro Jimenes and War Minister Desiderio Arias, US Marines landed and established control by May 15, 1916, aiming to force repayment of Dominican debts to European creditors whose governments were threatening intervention. The US military government built roads connecting Santo Domingo to Santiago, Azua and San Pedro de Macorís, created the Dominican Constabulary Guard to replace partisan militias, balanced the budget and reduced debt, while controlling Dominican finances through the National City Bank of New York.

A guerrilla resistance called the gavilleros, led by General Ramón Natera, fought the occupation from 1917 to 1922 in the eastern provinces, mostly armed with black-powder rifles against American artillery and, from 1919, Marine aircraft fitted with machine guns; a Congressional investigation found imprisoned guerrillas had been mistreated. Political pressure from Warren Harding's 1921 campaign led to the 1922 Hughes-Peynado agreement; after Horacio Vásquez won the March 1924 election, US forces withdrew on September 18, 1924, transferring police authority to the Dominican National Guard, the force a young officer named Rafael Trujillo would rise through.

He suffered a stroke in prison in 1956, was pardoned on 15 November 1964 and died on 21 April 1965; more than 75,000 Puerto Ricans accompanied his remains. trujillo-dictatorship-1930.summary: Rafael Trujillo, risen through the US-created National Guard, seized power in August 1930 and ruled the Dominican Republic for 31 years through a personality cult and a secret police that killed an estimated 25,000 to over 50,000 people, while promoting "dominicanidad," an official anti-Black, anti-Haitian national ideology, and "blanqueamiento," the whitening of the population.
account: Rafael Trujillo rose through the ranks of the US-created Dominican National Guard during the American occupation. In 1930 he made a secret arrangement with rebel leader Rafael Estrella Ureña: Trujillo kept his troops in their barracks while Estrella's forces marched on the capital, and Trujillo then stood for the presidency, officially winning with an implausible 99 percent of the vote. He renamed the capital Ciudad Trujillo and built a personality cult ("Dios y Trujillo"; churches required to display "God in Heaven, Trujillo on Earth"); government employees were required to donate 10 percent of their salaries to the state. His secret police, the SIM, killed an estimated 25,000 to over 50,000 opponents and civilians over his rule.

Trujillo's regime, initially backed by the United States, promoted "dominicanidad," an official ideology distinguishing Dominican from Haitian identity and portraying Haiti as a threat; his government rewrote Dominican history to cast Haitians as constant aggressors. He promoted "blanqueamiento," the whitening of the population, wore skin-lightening makeup himself, and had many Afro-Dominicans reclassified as "indio" to distance them from Blackness, even though his own grandmother was Haitian. This ideology directly preceded and justified his October 1937 Parsley Massacre of Haitians on the border.

Charges were finally dropped for four of the nine; the others received long sentences. On November 21, 2013, Alabama's parole board granted posthumous pardons to the three who had not yet been pardoned or had their convictions overturned.

rhoads-letter-puerto-rico-1931.summary: In November 1931 Rockefeller Institute pathologist Cornelius Rhoads wrote a letter from Puerto Rico calling Puerto Ricans a degenerate race and claiming he had killed eight and transplanted cancer into others; Pedro Albizu Campos made it public in 1932.
account: In 1931 Cornelius P. Rhoads joined the Rockefeller Anemia Commission at Presbyterian Hospital in San Juan, where the group had more than 200 patients, primarily clinical subjects. On November 10, 1931, he wrote an unmailed letter calling Puerto Ricans “the dirtiest, laziest, most degenerate and thievish race of men ever inhabiting this sphere” and claiming he had furthered their extermination by killing eight and transplanting cancer into several more.

In early 1932 a lab assistant gave the letter to the nationalist leader Pedro Albizu Campos, who publicized it and charged that Rhoads was part of a U.S. plot to exterminate Puerto Ricans. An investigation by the Puerto Rican Attorney General reviewed the files of 257 patients, including 13 who died, and found no evidence of the crimes described; Rhoads called his words a joke.

Rhoads went on to lead Memorial Hospital and Sloan-Kettering and appeared on the cover of Time in 1949. In 2002 an investigation led by Jay Katz for the American Association for Cancer Research found no evidence of unethical human experimentation but judged the letter so offensive that the association removed Rhoads's name from its award.

He calls them unfortunate subjects, not Israelites, not people of significance. And there were no reparations for Puerto Rico.

tuskegee-syphilis-study-1932.summary: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service began a study of untreated syphilis in 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, deceiving them and withholding treatment for forty years.
account: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service, working with the Tuskegee Institute, began a study to record the natural history of syphilis, the “Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male.” It enrolled 600 impoverished Black sharecroppers, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. Their informed consent was not collected; they were told they were being treated for “bad blood” and promised free medical care.

The men were told the study would last six months; it lasted forty years. By 1943 penicillin was the treatment of choice, and by 1947 it was standard, but the men were not offered it, and researchers kept them from treatment elsewhere.

The study ended in 1972 after an Associated Press story. By then 28 of the men had died of syphilis and 100 of related complications, 40 of their wives had been infected, and 19 of their children had been born with congenital syphilis. President Bill Clinton apologized on May 16, 1997.

points: The study was conducted from 1932 to 1972: the men were only told they were receiving free health care, and they were deceived with placebos disguised as treatment.

rastafari-leonard-howell-1933.summary: Leonard Percival Howell, deported from the United States in 1932 after working with Marcus Garvey's UNIA, began preaching in Jamaica from 1933 that the newly crowned Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie I was the returned Black Messiah, becoming one of the first teachers of what grew into the Rastafari movement; convicted of sedition for it, he went on to found the Pinnacle commune at Sligoville, St Catherine, in 1940, which the colonial and Jamaican authorities raided and eventually destroyed.
account: Howell, born in Clarendon, Jamaica, in 1898, migrated to the United States and became a lieutenant in Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association before being deported back to Jamaica in December 1932. Inspired by the November 1930 coronation of Ras Tafari Makonnen as Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia, Howell began preaching from January 1933 that Selassie was the incarnation of God and the returned Black Messiah for the African diaspora. He founded the King of Kings Mission, appointed himself Selassie's representative in Jamaica, and was prosecuted for sedition for preaching doctrines the colonial authorities judged anti-Church and anti-government; he wrote the movement's first text, 'The Promised Key', in prison.

In 1940 Howell founded Pinnacle, a communal settlement on about 400 acres at Sligoville in St Catherine Parish, where several hundred followers farmed, traded and governed themselves largely outside colonial authority. Jamaican police raided Pinnacle more than once in the years that followed and ultimately cleared and destroyed it in the 1950s; sources differ on the exact years of the later raids, Howell's further imprisonment and Pinnacle's final destruction (see disagreements). Howell died in Kingston in 1981.

Workers of the Lonquimay gold washings rose against the store's administration; President Arturo Alessandri Palma sent Carabineros and the army. 477 workers, many of them Mapuche, were killed, and around 500 prisoners taken.

account: By 1934 two-thirds of Indian land had passed into private ownership under the allotment begun by the General Allotment Act of 1887. The Meriam Report of 1928, 847 pages long, had condemned the poverty left by allotment and the conditions in the boarding schools. The Wheeler–Howard Act, signed by Roosevelt on June 18, 1934, was the chief work of Commissioner John Collier; Congress kept the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ oversight of tribes and reservations.

Each tribe had to vote within a year; abstentions were counted as yes votes, though among the Oglala Lakota abstaining had meant no. 172 tribes accepted the act and 75 rejected it Collier antagonized the Navajo, the largest tribe, who had been badly hurt by the federal livestock reduction program that took away half their livestock.

parsley-massacre-1937.summary: In October 1937 Dominican troops, on the orders of Rafael Trujillo, massacred Haitians living along the Dominican frontier; scholars generally estimate some 20,000 deaths.
account: The Parsley massacre was a mass killing of Haitians living in the Dominican Republic's northwestern frontier and parts of the Cibao region in October 1937, carried out by the Dominican Army on the orders of the dictator Rafael Trujillo. Virtually the entire Haitian population of the frontier was killed or forced to flee.

Estimates range from 14,000 to 40,000 Haitian men, women and children killed; scholars generally agree on about 20,000. The name comes from reports that troops demanded each victim say the Spanish word perejil ("parsley") as a shibboleth, though most scholars regard the parsley test as more myth than personal account.

trinidad-oilfield-riots-fyzabad-1937.summary: A strike called by the labour organiser Tubal Uriah "Buzz" Butler among Trinidad's oilfield workers on 18 June 1937 erupted into violence at Fyzabad when police tried to arrest him, killing a police corporal and sparking island-wide riots that left 14 dead and 59 wounded; Governor Arthur Fletcher declared a state of emergency, and British warships and troops suppressed the unrest by 6 July.
account: Tubal Uriah "Buzz" Butler organised an oil workers' strike at Trinidad Leaseholds' Forest Reserve field in southern Trinidad beginning 18 June 1937. The next day, when police tried to arrest Butler as he addressed a crowd at Fyzabad, his supporters stopped them; Police Corporal Charlie King, trying to make the arrest, was chased, thrown from a shop window, broke his leg, and was then burned to death by the crowd at Fyzabad Junction.

Fourteen people were killed and 59 wounded in the violence that followed at Fyzabad and across the colony. Governor Arthur Fletcher declared a state of emergency, and the British warships HMS Ajax and HMS Exeter arrived on 22–23 June with about 2,200 troops and police, who suppressed the unrest by 6 July. Butler was imprisoned from 9 September 1937 to May 1939; tried between 25 November and 16 December 1937, he was convicted of inciting to riot and sentenced to two years.

frome-and-kingston-riots-jamaica-1938.summary: Labour unrest that broke out at the Tate & Lyle-owned Frome sugar estate in Westmoreland in 1938 spread to Kingston and across Jamaica, leaving 46 dead and at least 429 injured; the unrest, part of a wave across the British West Indies from 1934 to 1939, led Britain to appoint the Moyne Commission, whose findings produced the Colonial Development and Welfare Act of 1940 and fed the rise of Jamaica's trade unions and political parties.
account: In the 1930s the British firm Tate & Lyle bought the Frome estate in Westmoreland, Jamaica, and in May 1937 formed the West Indies Sugar Company with £600,000 of capital, consolidating several plantations and leaving many sugar workers without jobs. That grievance fed labour riots at the Frome factory in 1938, where police killed four protesters and wounded nine; unrest spread from Frome east to Kingston, and across Jamaica the 1938 unrest left 46 dead and at least 429 injured, with thousands detained and prosecuted.

Jamaica's 1938 unrest was part of a wider wave of labour disturbances across the British West Indies from 1934 to 1939, including Trinidad's 1937 riots and a 1937 Barbados uprising that killed between 14 and 22 people. The British government responded by appointing the West India Royal Commission, chaired by Lord Moyne, which investigated conditions from November 1938 to February 1939 and reported on housing, agriculture, health, prisons and schools; its findings led to the Colonial Development and Welfare Act of July 1940, which committed £5 million a year for ten years to colonial development and £500,000 a year indefinitely for colonial research. The unrest also strengthened Jamaica's trade unions and fed the growth of the People's National Party (1938) and the Jamaica Labour Party (1943).

bracero-program-1942-1964.summary: From 1942 to 1964 the United States and Mexico ran the Bracero Program, the largest guest-worker program in U.S. history, issuing about 4.6 to 5 million contracts to Mexican farm and railroad laborers, many of whom never received the savings deducted from their pay.
account: The program began on August 4, 1942 with the Mexican Farm Labor Agreement and lasted 22 years, offering employment contracts to 4.6 million (elsewhere in the source, 5 million) braceros in 24 U.S. states. Braceros were promised adequate housing, food and sanitation and a minimum wage of 30 cents an hour, and protection from discrimination; bribery was a common way to get a contract.

Ten percent of their pay was deducted, from 1942 to 1948, for savings accounts they were legally guaranteed on returning to Mexico; many field-working braceros never received their savings, and their struggles and lawsuits for it went on into the 2000s.

operation-bootstrap-and-the-great-migrat.summary: From 1947 Puerto Rico's Operation Bootstrap lured U.S. corporations with tax exemptions and cheap labour, while planned emigration sent Puerto Ricans north by air: some 31,000 a year moved to New York from 1946 to 1950, in what is called the Great Migration.
account: In May 1947 Puerto Rico's legislature passed the Industrial Incentives Act, eliminating corporate taxes to draw U.S. investment, with a ten-year exemption from many taxes; the Administration of Economic Development encouraged factories, and the economy turned from agriculture to industry. According to Virginia Sánchez Korrol of the Center for Puerto Rican Studies, Bootstrap rested on three elements: industrialization by tax inducements to American corporations, a cheap labour pool educated in English under a U.S.-imposed curriculum, and the proposed emigration of over a third of the island's population.

Air travel was one of the principal factors in the largest wave of Puerto Rican migration to New York City in the 1950s, 'the Great Migration'; the decision to migrate was generally rooted in the island's poverty and in public policies that sanctioned migration. In 1948 the Migration Division of Puerto Rico's Department of Labor opened its office in New York. An estimated 31,000 migrants a year went to New York from 1946 to 1950; nearly 40,000 settled in the city in 1946 and 58,500 in 1952–53.
In New York, Lolita Lebrón recalled restaurant signs reading "No dogs or Puerto Ricans allowed."

windrush-generation-1948.summary: On 22 June 1948 the troopship HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury carrying 802 Caribbean migrants to Britain under the newly passed British Nationality Act 1948, which gave citizens of the UK's colonies the right to live and work in Britain; the ship's arrival, following smaller earlier sailings, became the iconic start of the postwar Caribbean community in Britain, remembered as the "Windrush generation."
account: The HMT Empire Windrush, a former German troopship travelling from Australia to England, docked at Kingston, Jamaica, where a newspaper advertisement had offered cheap passage to Britain; many of the 802 passengers who boarded were former servicemen hoping to rejoin the RAF, while others simply sought opportunity in England. The ship arrived at the port of Tilbury, near London, on 22 June 1948.

The migrants travelled under the British Nationality Act 1948, which had just granted citizenship of the United Kingdom and colonies, with the right of entry and settlement in Britain, to people throughout the colonies. Earlier, smaller ships had already brought Caribbean migrants — the SS Ormonde in March 1947 with 241 passengers and the SS Almanzora in December 1947 with 200 — but the Windrush's arrival became the enduring symbol of the start of Britain's postwar Caribbean community, and its passengers and those who followed in subsequent years came to be known as the "Windrush generation."

account: The Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR), led by Víctor Paz Estenssoro and Hernán Siles Zuazo, governed from 9 April 1952 until the coup of 4 November 1964. Under the slogans 'Agrarian reform' and 'Nationalization of mines', the Agrarian Reform Decree was signed at Ucureña, Cochabamba, on 2 August 1953; it granted hacienda lands to Indians through their unions and communities, on condition they not be sold individually. cuban-revolution-1953-1959.summary: After Fulgencio Batista's coup of 10 March 1952, Fidel Castro's attack on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953 began the revolution; Batista fled on 31 December 1958 and the 26th of July Movement took power on 1 January 1959.
account: On 10 March 1952 the army under Fulgencio Batista staged a coup ahead of the elections set for 1 June and established a de facto military dictatorship. On 26 July 1953 Fidel and Raúl Castro led an armed assault on the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba; it failed and the survivors were imprisoned, but the date gave its name to the 26th of July Movement.

Amnestied, the Castros went into exile in Mexico and returned in 1956 aboard the Granma with Che Guevara, reorganizing in the Sierra Maestra. termination-and-relocation-1953.summary: From 1953 Congress set out to end its recognition of the tribes: between 1953 and 1964 it terminated more than 100 tribes and bands, while the 1956 Relocation Act drew tens of thousands of Native people off the reservations into the cities.
account: House Concurrent Resolution 108 of August 1, 1953 announced the policy of termination: ending the tribes’ status as wards, the federal trust over reservations and the exclusion of state law. Public Law 280 the same year let states take jurisdiction over reservations. Between 1953 and 1964 more than 100 tribes and bands were terminated, affecting more than 12,000 Native people, 3% of the Native population.

The Indian Relocation Act, signed by Eisenhower on August 3, 1956, offered vocational training to draw Native people off the reservations into the cities; it has been characterized as part of the termination policy, weakening community and tribal ties. In 1950 only 6% of American Indians lived in urban areas; by 1960 more than 31,000 had moved to cities since 1952, about 30% of them returning, and some found poverty, joblessness and homelessness there instead of the promised help.

His murder is seen as a catalyst for the civil rights movement; the Emmett Till Antilynching Act became law on March 29, 2022.

duvalier-dynasty-haiti-1957-1986.summary: François "Papa Doc" Duvalier ruled Haiti from 1957 until his death in 1971 through the paramilitary Tonton Macoutes, declaring himself president for life in 1964; his son Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" succeeded him and ruled until a popular uprising forced him into exile in France on February 7, 1986.
account: François Duvalier was president of Haiti from October 22, 1957, until his death on April 21, 1971. In 1959 he formed the Militia of National Security Volunteers, known as the Tonton Macoutes, an unsalaried paramilitary and secret-police force that grew to roughly twice the size of the army by 1961 and eventually numbered in the hundreds of thousands; its members financed themselves through extortion and violence against Duvalier's opponents. In June 1964 a fraudulent referendum (reported as 99.9 percent in favor, with ballots premarked "yes") declared him president for life. Estimates of those killed or disappeared under his rule range from 30,000 to 60,000.

On Duvalier's death in 1971 his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier succeeded him and ruled for 15 more years, continuing widespread torture and killing while hundreds of thousands emigrated. Popular revolts beginning in Gonaïves in 1985 spread nationwide by early 1986; under pressure from the Reagan administration, Jean-Claude Duvalier fled Haiti for France aboard a U.S. Air Force aircraft on February 7, 1986, ending 29 years of Duvalier rule. He returned to Haiti in January 2011, was charged with corruption and human-rights abuses, and died in Haiti on October 4, 2014.

west-indies-federation-1958-1962.summary: The West Indies Federation, uniting ten British Caribbean territories under one government from 3 January 1958, collapsed after a September 1961 Jamaican referendum voted to leave; Jamaica's withdrawal on 6 August 1962 led Trinidad's premier Eric Williams to declare that "one from ten leaves nought," and the federation was formally dissolved on 31 May 1962.
account: The West Indies Federation was established on 3 January 1958, joining ten territories — Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, Antigua, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla, with the Cayman Islands and Turks and Caicos administratively attached to Jamaica — under a single federal government.

Jamaica, the largest member, resented having a smaller share of federal parliamentary seats than its population warranted and feared its bauxite wealth would be drained to support poorer members; many Jamaicans were also unhappy that Kingston was not made the federal capital. A September 1961 referendum produced a 54% vote to leave the federation, against the opposition of Jamaican premier Norman Manley. Jamaica formally withdrew on 6 August 1962, and Trinidad's premier, Eric Williams, responded that "one from ten leaves nought," judging the federation no longer viable without its two largest economies; it was formally dissolved on 31 May 1962.

united-states-embargo-against-cuba-1960.summary: After Cuba's nationalizations, the United States cut off trade from 1960 and in 1962 extended the embargo to almost all Cuban trade; reinforced in 1992 and 1996, it is the most enduring trade embargo in modern history and has been condemned by the UN General Assembly since 1992.
account: The U.S. launched an arms embargo against Cuba in 1958 and targeted its energy and agricultural sectors in 1960. After nationalizations and Cuba's seizure of American assets, including oil refineries, in October 1960, the U.S. retaliated with a total embargo on Cuban trade, with exceptions for food and medicine. The Foreign Assistance Act of 4 September 1961 authorized a complete trade embargo; on 7 September 1962 Kennedy formally expanded it to all Cuban trade except the non-subsidized sale of food and medicines, and the Cuban Assets Control Regulations followed on 8 July 1963.

The embargo was reinforced by the Cuban Democracy Act of 1992 and the Helms–Burton Act of 1996, which penalizes foreign companies that do business in Cuba. It was loosened during the thaw of 2015–2017 and tightened sharply thereafter. It is the most enduring trade embargo in modern history, and the United Nations has formally condemned it since 1992 for its impact on Cubans.

saint-lucia-independence-1979.summary: Saint Lucia, which changed hands between France and Britain roughly a dozen times during the 18th century before Britain secured permanent control in 1814, became independent from the United Kingdom on 22 February 1979 under Premier John Compton of the United Workers Party, who was defeated later that same year by Allan Louisy's Saint Lucia Labour Party.
account: During the 18th century Saint Lucia changed ownership, or was declared neutral territory, about a dozen times between France and Britain, earning it the name 'Helen of the West' after the mythological Helen of Troy. Britain secured permanent control in 1814 under the Treaty of Paris ending the Napoleonic Wars. The island was granted representative government in 1924, universal suffrage in 1951, and membership in the West Indies Federation from 1958 to 1962, followed by associated statehood with internal self-government in 1967.

Saint Lucia became independent on 22 February 1979 under Premier John Compton of the United Workers Party, remaining a Commonwealth realm. Compton's party was defeated later the same year by the Saint Lucia Labour Party under Allan Louisy.

account: The French first colonised Saint Vincent in 1719, settling at Barrouallie and importing enslaved Africans to work plantations. Britain captured the island during the Seven Years' War, with control confirmed by the 1763 Treaty of Paris. The Garifuna (Black Carib) people fought two wars against British control, the First Carib War of 1772-1773 and the Second Carib War of 1795-1797 led by paramount chief Joseph Chatoyer with French support; after their defeat in 1797, almost 5,000 Garifuna were deported to Roatan in Honduras, Belize, and Baliceaux in the Grenadines.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became fully independent from the United Kingdom on 27 October 1979, with Milton Cato of the centre-left Saint Vincent Labour Party, who had served as Premier since 1974, as its first prime minister; he ruled until his defeat in the 1984 general election.

grenada-revolution-and-us-invasion-1979-.summary: Maurice Bishop's New Jewel Movement took power in a nearly bloodless 1979 coup and built free health care and literacy programmes; after his deputy Bernard Coard's faction placed him under house arrest in October 1983, a crowd freed him but he and seven allies were executed by firing squad on 19 October, and the United States invaded Grenada on 25 October in an eight-day operation that deposed the new military government.
account: On 13 March 1979 Maurice Bishop led the New Jewel Movement in a nearly bloodless coup against Prime Minister Eric Gairy while Gairy was abroad, establishing a People's Revolutionary Government that suspended the constitution, detained political opponents, and built free health care and literacy programmes that drew international attention.

On 13 October 1983 a faction led by Bishop's deputy, Bernard Coard, placed Bishop under house arrest. On 19 October a crowd estimated at 15,000 to 30,000 freed him and marched with him to occupy Fort Rupert, but Bishop and seven allies were lined up in the fort's courtyard and executed by firing squad that same day; Hudson Austin then formed a military council to rule the island.

On 25 October 1983 the United States invaded Grenada in Operation Urgent Fury, an eight-day operation ending 2 November that involved about 7,300 US troops against roughly 1,300 Grenadian and 784 Cuban personnel (including 636 construction workers). The invasion killed 19 to 24 US troops, 24 Cubans, 21 to 45 Grenadians and 24 civilians (18 of them in the bombing of a mental hospital); 638 Cubans were captured. Hudson Austin's government was deposed, and Nicholas Brathwaite led the island until elections were held in December 1984.

points: Watching a video account of Maurice Bishop's rise and fall, the class affirms that he was a lawyer from Grenada who led a bloodless coup, built free health care and launched literacy programmes that brought down unemployment, and that his own revolutionary army, not a foreign enemy, carried out his 1983 execution.
In the class's understanding, the CIA was behind Bishop's execution by his own military, and the United States went to war with Grenada afterward.

The war of 1981–1990 killed 32,000–43,000 people; more than 600,000 were left homeless and 150,000 refugees fled to Costa Rica, Honduras and the United States.

Between 15 April and 31 October 1980 Cuban Americans organized boats from Mariel Harbor; the government treated the exodus as a social cleansing of 'undesirables' and organized acts of repudiation against those leaving. About 125,000 Cubans reached Florida.

Though the early waves of exiles were majority white, Afro-Cuban exiles became more common with Mariel: between 20% and 40% of the Marielitos were identified as black. Only 2.2 percent (2,746) were classified as serious or violent criminals under U.S. law. Many were held in detention; Mariel detainees at Oakdale and Atlanta prisons rioted in 1987 over deportations.

antigua-and-barbuda-independence-1981.summary: Antigua and Barbuda became independent from the United Kingdom on 1 November 1981, with Vere Cornwall Bird sworn in as its first prime minister, after a constitutional process in which the British refused Barbuda's bid to separate from Antigua as its own territory and instead gave Barbuda increased local autonomy.
account: Antigua, an associated state of the United Kingdom from 1967, moved toward full independence after its government signalled the intention in 1978 and the pro-independence party won 13 of 17 seats in the April 1980 election. A constitutional conference at Lancaster House in December 1980 addressed outstanding issues, including a Barbudan delegation's wish to separate from Antigua as its own territory, which the British refused on grounds of Barbuda's small population; the compromise instead amended the Barbuda Local Government Act to give the island greater autonomy.

Antigua's House of Representatives passed a resolution consenting to the termination of its association with Britain on 23 April 1981, and the Senate passed it on 1 May 1981. The British House of Lords approved the independence order on 8 July 1981 by a vote of 75 to 7, and Queen Elizabeth II signed both the termination and constitution orders on 31 July 1981. Antigua and Barbuda became independent on 1 November 1981, and Vere Cornwall Bird was sworn in as its first prime minister.

account: On August 18, 1996 the San Jose Mercury News began the three-part 'Dark Alliance' series. It reported that a Bay Area drug ring sold tons of cocaine to Los Angeles gangs and funneled profits to the Contras, and told how Ricky Donnell Ross rose to be one of the largest cocaine dealers in southern California, supplied by Oscar Danilo Blandón and Norwin Meneses, men with ties to the FDN Contra group.

Earlier reports (an Associated Press article of December 20, 1985 and Senate hearings in the late 1980s) had alleged Contra ties to drug trafficking. Many readers took the series to claim that the CIA was responsible for the crack epidemic; the Washington Post, Los Angeles Times and New York Times disputed this, and the Mercury News's own editor later wrote that the series had implied more than it proved. The Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General reviewed the allegations in a 1997 report.

account: Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla became an associated state of the United Kingdom with full internal self-government in 1967. Anguilla, resentful of domination by St Kitts, unilaterally declared independence from the arrangement that same year and was formally separated from it in 1980, remaining a British overseas territory. A constitutional conference was held in London in 1982; the resulting Constitution of Saint Kitts and Nevis was adopted on 23 June 1983, giving Nevis the right to secede from the federation if a referendum produced a two-thirds majority in favour.

Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent on 19 September 1983, with Dr Kennedy Simmonds, who had served as Premier since 1980, as its first prime minister. The new country opted to remain within the Commonwealth, with the British monarch as head of state represented by a Governor-General.

Robinson and most of his National Alliance for Reconstruction cabinet hostage, while 72 others attacked the Trinidad and Tobago Television (TTT) station. Twenty-four people died in the uprising, and the government later estimated millions of dollars in property losses from the accompanying looting and arson. haitian-boat-people-guantanamo-1991-1994.summary: After the September 1991 coup against Jean-Bertrand Aristide, the US Coast Guard interdicted tens of thousands of Haitians fleeing by boat and, under a policy upheld by the Supreme Court in 1993, returned most of them to Haiti without a hearing; those found HIV-positive were instead held for up to twenty months behind razor wire at Guantánamo Bay until a federal court ordered the camp closed in June 1993.
account: Under a 1981 US-Haitian agreement, the US Coast Guard intercepted vessels carrying undocumented Haitians and screened passengers at sea for asylum claims before returning the rest to Haiti. After the September 1991 military coup against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, the number of Haitians fleeing by boat rose sharply, overwhelming the screening capacity on Coast Guard cutters; thousands were instead taken to a tent camp at the US Naval Base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for processing.

In 1992, the Bush administration ordered the Coast Guard to repatriate intercepted Haitians directly to Haiti without any screening for asylum claims, a policy the incoming Clinton administration continued. Haitians who tested positive for HIV were segregated from the rest of the Guantánamo camp and held in a separate, fenced compound -- the only known refugee camp in the world made up entirely of HIV-positive detainees -- some for as long as twenty months.

The Haitian Centers Council and other plaintiffs sued over conditions at the HIV camp; on June 8, 1993, federal judge Sterling Johnson Jr. ordered the camp closed, writing that although the government called it a "humanitarian camp," it was in substance "an HIV prison camp," and ordered the remaining detainees released into the United States. Separately, in Sale v. Haitian Centers Council (decided June 21, 1993), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that the President's power to order the Coast Guard to repatriate undocumented aliens intercepted on the high seas was not limited by US immigration law or international refugee conventions; Justice Blackmun dissented alone.

views: The Supreme Court majority in Sale v. Haitian Centers Council (1993) held that neither US immigration law nor the UN Refugee Convention's non-return provision applied to people intercepted outside US territory.

Justice Blackmun's dissent, and the plaintiffs in the Guantánamo HIV-camp litigation, argued the policy amounted to forced repatriation of refugees in substance, regardless of where on the water they were stopped.

account: On April 7, 2003, Haitian President Jean-Bertrand Aristide formally demanded that France pay Haiti restitution of over $21 billion, which he said was the equivalent in present-day money of the 90 million gold francs Haiti had been forced to pay Paris after winning its independence. French and Haitian officials later told the New York Times that Aristide's reparations push was a factor driving French and American cooperation on removing him, since France feared that paying reparations to Haiti would set a precedent for claims from other former colonies such as Algeria. Aristide was flown out of the country in the February 2004 coup; Haiti's transitional prime minister, Gerard Latortue, called the reparations claim "illegal" and "ridiculous" and the demand was dropped.

hurricane-jeanne-haiti-2004.summary: Although its center passed north of Haiti, Hurricane Jeanne dropped heavy rain from September 17 to 19, 2004 that flooded the deforested hillsides above Gonaïves under 16 feet of water, killing roughly 3,000 people nationwide -- most of them in that one city -- just months after the February 2004 coup that drove Jean-Bertrand Aristide from office.
account: Hurricane Jeanne passed north of Haiti in September 2004 without making landfall there, but its outer bands dropped roughly 330 millimeters of rain over about 36 hours, from September 17 to 19. Decades of deforestation had stripped the hillsides above the port city of Gonaïves of the tree cover that would otherwise have slowed the runoff, and floodwaters reaching about 16 feet deep inundated roughly 80 percent of the city of around 100,000 people.

Haiti's Directorate of Civil Protection and international relief agencies recorded approximately 3,006 deaths nationwide, with 2,826 of them in Gonaúves alone, making Jeanne one of the deadliest Atlantic hurricanes on record for Haiti. About 5,490 homes were destroyed across the country, and roughly 300,000 people were left homeless in the Nord-Ouest department.

The flooding struck seven months after the armed rebellion that forced President Jean-Bertrand Aristide from office in February 2004, while the country was still under a transitional government and the newly arrived UN peacekeeping mission (MINUSTAH), compounding a humanitarian crisis already underway.

haiti-earthquake-2010.summary: A magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck near Léogâne, 25 kilometers from Port-au-Prince, on January 12, 2010; estimates of the dead range from about 46,000 to over 300,000, some 1.5 million people were displaced, and the American Red Cross was later found to have built only six houses in Haiti despite raising almost $500 million.
account: On January 12, 2010, at 16:53 local time, a magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck roughly 25 kilometers west of Port-au-Prince near Léogâne, at a depth of 13 kilometers. Death-toll estimates vary enormously by source: the Haitian government cited 220,000 to 316,000; the Inter-American Development Bank estimated 200,000-250,000 in February 2010; a University of Michigan study put it near 160,000; a Radio Netherlands investigation found about 92,000; and a 2011 USAID draft report estimated 46,000-85,000. A UN official said at the time, "I do not think we will ever know what the death toll is from this earthquake." The International Federation of Red Cross estimated 3 million people affected; USAID put displacement at about 1.5 million, with 550,000 still without permanent shelter as of January 2012. Total damage was estimated at $7.8-8.5 billion, with roughly 250,000 homes and 30,000 commercial buildings destroyed or severely damaged.

An NPR/ProPublica investigation published in June 2015 found that the American Red Cross raised nearly $488 million for Haiti earthquake relief but built only six permanent homes, despite initially planning about 700; much of the money went to other organizations that took their own overhead, and the Red Cross disputed the account.

account: The first confirmed cholera case in Haiti's modern history was recorded on October 21, 2010, nine months after the January earthquake, with the outbreak spreading rapidly along the Artibonite River. Investigators, including journalist Jonathan M. Katz and epidemiologist Renaud Piarroux, traced the source to a UN base housing Nepalese peacekeepers whose waste from outhouses flowed into the Artibonite; DNA testing matched the outbreak strain to those found in South Asia. By 2013 more than 6 percent of Haiti's population had been infected; the outbreak eventually accounted for an estimated 820,000 cases and nearly 10,000 deaths, and represented 57 percent of all cholera cases and 45 percent of all cholera deaths recorded worldwide in 2010-2011.

The United Nations resisted acknowledging responsibility for years. In December 2016, Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon formally apologized and pledged $400 million toward a response, though only a small fraction of that pledge had materialized in the years that followed.

dominican-nationality-ruling-2013.summary: The Dominican Republic's Constitutional Court ruled in 2013 that anyone born after 1929 to parents the state classified as "in transit," overwhelmingly Dominicans of Haitian descent, had never held Dominican nationality, rendering an estimated 200,000 people stateless; a 2014 law offered a path to regularize some of them.
account: In Sentencia TC/0168/13, the Dominican Republic's Constitutional Court ruled that anyone born in the country after June 21, 1929 to foreign parents classified as "in transit" -- a category long applied to undocumented Haitian laborers regardless of how many years or generations they had lived in the country -- had never legally held Dominican nationality, and ordered authorities to audit birth records back to that date. An estimated 200,000 people, overwhelmingly of Haitian descent, faced statelessness as a result; Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights all condemned the ruling.

In response, the government passed Law 169-14 in 2014, creating two categories: about 55,000 people with Civil Registry birth records received an amnesty and Dominican identity documents; about 53,000 people without such records had to register as foreigners and apply to naturalize by a 2015 deadline, of whom only 8,755 successfully registered. A further group born 2007-2010 had to register as foreigners and could seek ordinary naturalization after two years.

puerto-rico-debt-crisis-and-promesa-2014.summary: When Puerto Rico's bonds were cut to junk in 2014, Congress passed PROMESA in 2016 and set over the island a federally appointed oversight board, 'la junta', which cut health care, pensions and education to repay creditors; students struck against a $450 million cut to the university in 2017.
account: The crisis began in 2014 when three major credit agencies downgraded Puerto Rico's bonds to junk status. In 2016 Congress enacted PROMESA, a custom-made bankruptcy law that established a Financial Oversight and Management Board, known in Puerto Rico as 'la junta', with ultimate control over the Commonwealth's budget; all seven voting members were appointed by the U.S. President. Governor García Padilla suspended payments due on 1 July 2016.

The board's austerity plan for 2017–2026 cut deeply into health care, pensions and education. By May 2017 the government and its corporations owed $123 billion, and the board sought a federal judge for 'the largest bankruptcy case in the history of the American public bond market'; a 2018 report counted $74 billion in bond debt and $49 billion in unfunded pensions. Puerto Rico exited bankruptcy on 15 March 2022.

On 28 March 2017 students at the University of Puerto Rico's Río Piedras campus began a strike against a $450 million budget cut to the public university under PROMESA; it spread to most of the system's eleven campuses and ended on 7 June 2017.

standing-rock-dakota-access-2016.summary: From April 2016 thousands joined the Standing Rock Sioux to stop the Dakota Access Pipeline under Lake Oahe, near their water source and sacred sites; protesters were met with attack dogs, pepper spray and water cannon, and the camps were cleared in February 2017.
account: The pipeline runs from North Dakota’s Bakken oil fields to Illinois, crossing under Lake Oahe near the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation; the tribe feared for the Missouri River, its water source, and for sacred and burial sites. In April 2016 youth from Standing Rock began a campaign to stop it. On September 3, 2016 the company bulldozed ground the tribe had identified as containing possible burial sites; private security used attack dogs and pepper spray, and at least six protesters were treated for dog bites. A United Nations expert said the tribe had been excluded from consultation.

In November 2016 police used tear gas and water cannon on protesters in freezing weather. On December 4, 2016 the Army said it would not grant the easement under Lake Oahe, but in early 2017 the Army Corps of Engineers granted it. The last protesters were evicted by the National Guard and police on February 23, 2017.

splc-lists-iuic-as-hate-group-2016.summary: The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) listed Israel United in Christ among active hate groups in its annual reports for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2021 and 2022; IUIC denies it is a hate group.
account: The SPLC, a nonprofit legal advocacy organization in Montgomery, Alabama, has published an annual census of hate groups since 1990. Its report “Active Hate Groups in the United States in 2015,” published February 4, 2016, included Israel United in Christ among its black separatist and black nationalist groups, and IUIC appears in the SPLC’s lists for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2021 and 2022. In 2008 the SPLC had written that “the extremist fringe of the Hebrew Israelite movement” had a Black supremacist outlook, while also writing that “most Hebrew Israelites are neither explicitly racist nor anti-Semitic and do not advocate violence.”

In 2019 Heidi Beirich of the SPLC told the BBC that the center lists IUIC as a “black nationalist hate group” and “racist”: “racist against white people, racist against Jews,” and “incredibly homophobic, as well.” The Oklahoman reported in 2022 that the SPLC designated IUIC a hate group “notably due to what the nonprofit law center described as the group’s anti-white, anti-Semitic and anti-LGBTQ messaging,” and placed it among groups espousing “Radical Hebrew Israelites” ideology.

IUIC denies that it is a hate group. It told the BBC that “at no point do we teach against the laws of the land or authorities.” Bishop Kani told The Oklahoman the group had been “mislabeled”: “We don’t promote violence, we’re not out there looking to harm people… they translate when we talk as hate because we’re trying to empower ourselves.” Many of IUIC’s videos open with the disclaimer “We are not a hate group,” and its website tells members to notify the authorities of any plot to cause harm or break the laws of the land.

points: Once a group is put on the hate list, it becomes a target: every IUIC branch is listed with its address and phone number, so that somebody will come in and do something. That is why the schools keep security.

account: DAMN., Kendrick Lamar’s fourth studio album, was released on April 14, 2017. The song “Fear” opens with a voicemail from Lamar’s cousin Karni Israel Duckworth (then Carl Duckworth), a member of the Black Hebrew Israelites, reciting Deuteronomy 28:28. In a second voicemail at the end of the song he says: “The so-called Blacks, Hispanics, and Native American Indians are the true children of Israel. We are the Israelites, according to the Bible. The children of Israel. He’s gonna punish us for our iniquities, for our disobedience because we chose to follow other gods.” On “Yah” Lamar says, “I’m an Israelite, don’t call me Black no more.”

The album debuted at the top of the Billboard 200 with 603,000 album-equivalent units in its first week and earned Lamar the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Music, the first time the prize went to an artist outside classical music and jazz. haiti-petrocaribe-protests-2018-2019.summary: A Haitian Senate probe found that officials across three administrations, including then-president Jovenel Moïse, had embezzled an estimated 3.8 billion dollars raised through Venezuela's discounted PetroCaribe oil program; a viral #PetroCaribeChallenge launched in August 2018 by Gilbert Mirambeau Jr. helped drive waves of protest in October-November 2018 and again in 2019 that killed dozens and nearly toppled Moïse's government.
account: Haiti joined the Venezuelan-financed PetroCaribe program, which let member states buy oil on credit at below-market rates and redirect the savings toward development projects. A Haitian Senate investigation released in November 2017, covering the years 2008 to 2016, found an estimated 3.8 billion dollars of PetroCaribe funds had been embezzled or misused by officials spanning three presidential administrations, including then-president Jovenel Moïse's own company.

On August 14, 2018, Haitian-Canadian activist Gilbert Mirambeau Jr. tweeted a photo of himself blindfolded holding a sign reading, in Haitian Creole, "Kot kòb PetwoKaribe a?" ("Where is the PetroCaribe money?"), launching the #PetroCaribeChallenge that spread rapidly online and became the public face of Haiti's anti-corruption movement.

Fuel-price increases in July 2018 had already triggered unrest; anger over the PetroCaribe revelations then drove protests through the autumn, including a week of demonstrations in November 2018 that left about 10 people dead. Haiti's Superior Court of Auditors released further findings in early 2019 documenting payments for projects that were never built, contracts awarded in a dead person's name, and large undocumented disbursements to officials, igniting a fresh wave of protests from February through October 2019 that the United Nations said killed at least 42 people and injured 86 between mid-September and October alone.

joy-morgan-murder-and-coverage-2019.summary: Joy Morgan, a 20-year-old midwifery student and member of IUIC’s UK branch, was murdered after a church celebration on December 26, 2018; fellow member Shohfah-El Israel was convicted on August 5, 2019, and coverage of the case carried her family’s and the SPLC’s charges against the church, which IUIC denied.
account: Joy Morgan, born February 12, 1998, was a midwifery student at the University of Hertfordshire. She joined the UK branch of Israel United in Christ in Ilford, east London, in January 2016, ran its children’s group, and two weeks before she went missing said in a video, “IUIC is my family and like the best family that I’ve ever had.” She was last seen alive on December 26, 2018 at a church celebration in Ilford. She was reported missing on February 7, 2019, after her housemates had not seen her since Christmas.

Police arrested fellow member Shohfah-El Israel (born Ajibola Shogbamimu) on February 9, 2019 on the M25; he was charged with murder on February 27. He admitted spending two nights alone with her at his Cricklewood flat, which broke the church’s rule against women being alone with men other than their husbands. A jury at Reading Crown Court convicted him on August 5, 2019, and he was sentenced to life with a minimum of 17 years; he refused to say where her body was. Her remains were found in woodland near Stevenage in October 2019. A 2021 coroner’s inquest could not establish how she died.

The coverage carried charges against the church. Her mother Carol said her daughter had been turned into a racist by the church and called it a cult, and her family said she had grown distant and called her mixed-race younger sister a “demon” and a “white devil.” Former members told the BBC of harsh discipline and of being told to cut off unbelieving family. The prosecutor described a strict hierarchy in which women had no rank. The SPLC described IUIC as a “hate group” and “a black nationalist group.”

IUIC denied these claims. It told the BBC that former members who speak against it are “disgruntled,” that claims it encourages members to cut off their families are “lies,” and that “at no point do we teach against the laws of the land or authorities.” The church described Shohfah-El Israel as an “enthusiastic” member and said he had once been demoted from the rank of soldier over his behaviour. Evidence given at the trial indicated that Joy Morgan had a good relationship with the church and its congregants, and police found no reliable indication that she wanted to leave it.

mapuche-conflict-and-the-plurinational-v.summary: Mapuche communities' struggle for their ancestral lands, lost in the Occupation of Araucanía, sharpened after police shot Camilo Catrillanca in 2018 and Chile sent troops to Biobío and Araucanía in 2021; in 2022 voters rejected, 61.89% to 38.11%, a constitution that would have made Chile a plurinational state.
account: The Mapuche conflict intensified with the return of democracy in the 1990s, as activists sought to recover the 'ancestral territory' lost in the Occupation of Araucanía and the Conquest of the Desert; its period of violence began in December 1997, and some groups have used violent tactics since 1998 while others negotiate. In 1993 the Chilean government passed the Indigenous Peoples Act recognizing Mapuche land, cultural and development rights. In 2018 Camilo Catrillanca, grandson of a local Indigenous leader, was shot in the head during a police operation near Ercilla; in October 2021 President Sebastián Piñera declared a state of emergency and deployed troops to Biobío and Araucanía.

The constitution drafted after the 2020 plebiscite declared that 'Chile is a Plurinational and Intercultural State'; the plurinational state and indigenous justice were among its most debated provisions. On 4 September 2022 it was rejected by 61.89% to 38.11%, winning also in communes with large indigenous populations, and the 1980 constitution of the dictatorship era remained in force.

mcgirt-v-oklahoma-2020.summary: On July 9, 2020 the Supreme Court held that the reservation promised to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and remains Indian country, so Oklahoma could not prosecute Native people for major crimes there.
account: Before statehood in 1907 about half of Oklahoma, including Tulsa, belonged to the Five Tribes: the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek and Seminole. The case was brought by Jimcy McGirt, an enrolled member of the Seminole tribe. Writing for a 5–4 majority, Justice Gorsuch held that the Muscogee domain remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act: “Because Congress has not said otherwise, we hold the government to its word.” He rejected the argument that “the price of keeping” the promises “has become too great.”

Oklahoma’s Court of Criminal Appeals applied McGirt to rule that nine other nations’ reservations had not been disestablished, but held it was not retroactive. In Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) the Supreme Court held that the state shares jurisdiction over crimes by non-Natives against Natives in Indian country.
